topics.summary: भूतानि, जिज्ञासा (revisited), उत्पत्तिक्रमम्, ओषधीनाम्.

concepts.title: भूतानि — All Living Beings

explanations.kidFriendly: भूतानि means 'all living beings' — every creature that lives. Glossary: प्राणिनः ('living ones'). The chapter's title says all of them arise from food.
explanations.textbook: भूतानि — 'beings/creatures', glossed प्राणिनः. Nominative plural of भूत (neuter past-participle 'become').
explanations.expert: भूतानि is a beautiful Sanskrit usage: 'beings' = 'those that have become' (past-participle of भू, 'to be'). Existence itself is described as a 'having-become'. The same word covers humans, animals, plants — every living being.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter's central claim — 'from food, all भूतानि come to be' — only works because भूतानि means EVERY living being, not just humans.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet भूतानि in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 9; the glossary gives 'All living beings'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see भूतानि, recall it means 'All living beings'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using भूतानि ('All living beings').

concepts.beyondTheBook: भूत carries multiple senses across Sanskrit: 'past' (in तेन भूतेन कालेन, 'in the past time'), 'being/creature' (पञ्चभूत = the five elements), and 'spirit/ghost' (Hindi भूत). All trace to the same root भू, 'to be'.

concepts.title: जिज्ञासा — Curiosity (returns!)

explanations.oneLine: जिज्ञासा (jijñāsā) — 'the wish to know' (returns from Chapter 1 — same word, same meaning).
explanations.kidFriendly: जिज्ञासा appears again — the wish to know that drives a student. In this chapter, someone's जिज्ञासा about the order of creation sparks the lesson. Glossary: ज्ञातुम् इच्छा.
explanations.textbook: जिज्ञासा — 'desire to know'. The chapter uses it (as in Ch.1 and Ch.7) for the curiosity that drives a learner. The same word, the same desiderative formation from ज्ञा.
explanations.expert: जिज्ञासा is the desiderative noun from ज्ञा (wish-to-know) — recognising it across chapters builds your sense of Sanskrit's productive grammar. Sister words: पिपासा (wish-to-drink), बुभुक्षा (wish-to-eat), चिकित्सा (wish-to-cure).

concepts.reasoning: The chapter shows that genuine learning starts with जिज्ञासा — the willingness to ASK why beings come from food and where it all begins.

useCases.title: Familiar pattern
useCases.description: ज्ञा + desiderative + -आ = जिज्ञासा ('wish to know').

useCases.title: Family of words
useCases.description: Same pattern: पिपासा (thirst), बुभुक्षा (hunger), चिकित्सा (wish to cure).

useCases.title: Curiosity-driven
useCases.description: The chapter's lesson begins because someone is curious — that is good Sanskrit pedagogy.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Recognising जिज्ञासा/पिपासा/बुभुक्षा as ONE pattern (desiderative-noun-of-X) is one of those moments where Sanskrit's regularity rewards you across many chapters.

concepts.title: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् — The Order of Origin

explanations.oneLine: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् (utpatti-kramam) — 'the order/sequence in which things come into being'.
explanations.kidFriendly: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् means the order/sequence of origination — the step-by-step chain of how things come to be. The chapter teaches the उत्पत्तिक्रमम्: food → beings → rain → yajna → action. Glossary: उत्पत्तेः क्रमम् ('the sequence of origin').
explanations.textbook: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् — 'order of origination', glossed उत्पत्तेः क्रमम्. A neuter accusative form (the object of जानीयात्).
explanations.expert: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् = उत्पत्ति ('arising, origination', उत् + पद् 'to step up') + क्रमम् ('order, sequence'). The Gītā's verse is exactly this — the सूचिका of how things arise in order.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses उत्पत्तिक्रमम् as the name for the chain it teaches — the ordered sequence of creation.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet उत्पत्तिक्रमम् in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 9; the glossary gives 'Order of origin'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see उत्पत्तिक्रमम्, recall it means 'Order of origin'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using उत्पत्तिक्रमम् ('Order of origin').

concepts.beyondTheBook: Sanskrit philosophy is very fond of क्रम (order/sequence): सृष्टिक्रम (order of creation), प्रलयक्रम (order of dissolution), कर्मक्रम (order of action). Naming a sequence makes it teachable.

concepts.title: ओषधीनाम् — Of Herbs

explanations.kidFriendly: ओषधीनाम् means 'of the herbs' — the genitive plural of ओषधि. The chapter mentions ओषधीनाम् as part of the chain of life — plants/herbs as a key link between rain and beings. Glossary: औषधोपयोगिपादपानाम् ('of medicinally-useful plants').
explanations.textbook: ओषधीनाम् — genitive plural of ओषधि ('herb, medicinal plant'), glossed औषधोपयोगि-पादपानाम्. The case ending -आनाम् is the standard feminine ī-stem genitive plural.
explanations.expert: ओषधि literally suggests plants that 'hold (धि-) heat/efficacy (ओष-)' — i.e. potent, medicinal plants. The Sanskrit medical tradition (Āyurveda) catalogues thousands of ओषधि; the same word survives in modern Hindi/Sanskrit for medicinal herbs.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter ties ओषधीनाम् (herbs) into the cycle of creation — they connect rain to food to living beings.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet ओषधीनाम् in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 9; the glossary gives 'Of herbs'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see ओषधीनाम्, recall it means 'Of herbs'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using ओषधीनाम् ('Of herbs').

concepts.beyondTheBook: The plant chapter of Sanskrit knowledge — from the Vedas through Caraka and Suśruta — is the world's longest continuous herbal medical tradition; ओषधि is its core word.

solutionSteps: Glossary: भूतानि = प्राणिनः ('living ones').
Past-participle of भू, 'beings/those that have become'.
commonMistakes: भूतानि is BEINGS, not foods or clouds — the verse says all beings come FROM food.

questions.prompt: 'जिज्ञासा' appears in this chapter again — it means —
solutionSteps: Glossary: जिज्ञासा = ज्ञातुम् इच्छा ('the wish to know').
Desiderative noun from ज्ञा — the same word as in Chapter 1.
commonMistakes: जिज्ञासा is CURIOSITY (wish to know), familiar from Chapter 1.

questions.prompt: 'जानीयात्' is in which mood — and what does it convey?
solutionSteps: Glossary: जानीयात् = अवगच्छेत् ('should understand').
Optative ending -यात् = 'ought to' — Sanskrit's polite moral 'should'.
commonMistakes: जानीयात् is OPTATIVE ('should know'), not a strict command — see the -यात् ending.

solutionSteps: Glossary: ओषधीनाम् = औषधोपयोगि-पादपानाम् ('of medicinally-useful plants').
Genitive plural of ओषधि ('medicinal herb').
commonMistakes: ओषधि is a HERB / medicinal plant — the same root behind Hindi औषधि (medicine).

glossary.definition: From Food, Beings Come To Be.
glossary.example: अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि — 'from food, beings come into being'; the chapter's title and the opening line of Gītā 3.14.
ब्रह्म (brahma) — 'the all-pervading Cosmic Power; the ultimate source of all'.
रसायनशास्त्रम् (rasāyana-śāstram) — 'chemistry'; the chapter explicitly mentions modern chemistry.
जानीयात् (jānīyāt) — 'one should know'; the optative case used for advice/duty.
जिज्ञासा (jijñāsā) — 'the wish to know' (returns from Chapter 1 — same word, same meaning).
उत्पत्तिक्रमम् (utpatti-kramam) — 'the order/sequence in which things come into being'.
ओषधीनाम् (oṣadhīnām) — 'of the herbs (medicinal plants)'.

misconceptions.actually: Classical Sanskrit भूतानि = 'beings, creatures' (every living thing). Same root (भू, 'to be') but two different uses. In Vedānta/Gītā context भूतानि = beings; in folk-Hindi भूत = ghost (a specific kind of being). Context dictates.
More precisely: 'FROM food, beings COME-TO-BE'. The food is the source, not a maker. Sanskrit ablatives express 'arise from', not 'are made by'. The chain (food → beings) is dependence, not creation.

यज्ञ = Vedic fire-ritual (often with offerings). पूजा = devotional worship (often image-based). Two different ritual traditions. In the Gītā verse, यज्ञ is the broader concept of selfless action including ritual. पूजा is the personal/temple worship form.

ज्ञेयः is a GERUNDIVE: 'should be known' / 'is to be known'. Sanskrit -य suffix on past-participial bases makes 'to-be-X-ed'. कृत = done; कार्य = to be done. ज्ञात = known; ज्ञेय = to be known. Big shift in meaning.

misconceptions.kidsThink: The -द् ending might look like an agent.
misconceptions.actually: अन्नाद् is ablative of अन्न: 'FROM food'. Final -द is the ablative ending of अन्न after sandhi. Sanskrit sandhi: अन्नात् + भवन्ति → अन्नाद्भवन्ति (the त् of -आत् becomes voiced -द् before the voiced भ्). Recognise sandhi rules and the case stays visible.

ncertQA.question: 'अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि' इत्यस्य कोऽर्थः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: अन्नात् भूतानि भवन्ति — From food, beings come to be. Bhagavad Gītā 3.14a. अन्नात् (ablative, 'from food') + भवन्ति ('they come to be', 3rd-pl present of भू) + भूतानि ('beings', neuter plural).

ncertQA.question: भूतानि कुतः भवन्ति? अन्नं कुतः भवति? पर्जन्यः कुतः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: भूतानि अन्नात्; अन्नं पर्जन्यात्; पर्जन्यः यज्ञात्; यज्ञः कर्मणः। (Gītā 3.14) The full verse names the chain: beings ← food ← rain ← yajña ← action. कर्म → यज्ञ → पर्जन्य → अन्न → भूत. Reverse the chain and the world's interdependence becomes visible.

ncertQA.question: 'ब्रह्म' इति पाठे कः अर्थः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: सर्वव्याप्तः परमेश्वरः। (the all-pervading Cosmic Power) Glossary: ब्रह्म = समष्टि-चितिशक्तिः / सर्वव्याप्तः परमेश्वरः. Neuter — the impersonal Absolute of Vedānta. Distinct from masculine ब्रह्मा (the creator-god) and ब्रह्मन् (a priest).

ncertQA.question: 'रसायनशास्त्रम्' इत्यस्य कोऽर्थः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: रसशास्त्रम् / chemistry. The chapter uses the modern Sanskrit term for chemistry — an old word (रसायन, originally meaning Āyurvedic tonics) reused for the modern subject. शास्त्रम् = 'science / treatise'.

ncertQA.question: 'जानीयात्' इति किम् रूपम्? तस्य कोऽर्थः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: विधिलिङ्-लकारस्य प्रथमपुरुष-एकवचनम् ('one should know'). 3rd-singular optative of ज्ञा. Glossary: जानीयात् = अवगच्छेत्. The optative mood (विधिलिङ्) expresses 'should / ought to', Sanskrit's gentle moral 'should'.

scientists.name: Veda Vyāsa
scientists.lifespan: traditional figure of pre-Common-Era India (specific dates uncertain)
scientists.oneLineLegacy: Traditionally credited with compiling the Vedas, composing the Mahābhārata, and (within the Mahābhārata) the Bhagavad Gītā.
scientists.narrative: Veda Vyāsa ('Vyāsa the compiler-of-Vedas') is the mythical-historical figure to whom Indian tradition attributes the organisation of the four Vedas, the composition of the eighteen Purāṇas, and the authorship of the Mahābhārata. The Bhagavad Gītā — including the chapter's verse 3.14 about the food-and-being chain — sits within the Mahābhārata. Scholars treat 'Vyāsa' as more a literary figure than a single historical person; the works attributed to him likely accreted over many centuries. But the role Vyāsa plays in the Indian imagination is real: the great organiser of the inheritance of wisdom.

miniProjects.title: Trace One Meal Back to the Soil
needs: One meal you eat this week
steps: Pick one item from your plate (say rice or dal).
Trace it back: where did this come from? (Shop → wholesaler → farmer → field).
What did the field need? (Soil, sun, rain, work).
What did the rain need? (Clouds, oceans, the water cycle).
Draw a chain (5 steps) on paper. Pin it to the fridge.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: Your chart traces from your fork back to the sun and rain. Looking at your plate becomes a different experience after this exercise.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: The Gītā 3.14 chain is not abstract — it is a description of where your lunch came from. The verse becomes useful when you DO it, not when you just read it.

whatIfs.question: Modern climate change makes this scenario very real.
whatIfs.answer: The chain food→beings would continue for a while on stored grain, but rain→food fails (drought), then beings starve. The Gītā does not say WHO breaks the chain, but the verse implies that the break starts from human कर्म (action). The 21st century has been demonstrating exactly this dynamic — human carbon, less rain, less food, more suffering. Old verse, current science.

whatIfs.question: Krishna's verse says action → yajña → rain → food → beings. Imagine humans STOPPED doing anything.
whatIfs.answer: Literally read, yes. The verse claims all of creation depends on humans participating in the cycle. Modern ecology would say the rain doesn't actually need human action — the water cycle is fine without us. But the verse's spiritual point is different: humans who do not ACT do not deserve to consume. It is an ethic about the right to eat.

whatIfs.question: Imagine the verse said simply action → rain → food → beings, with no यज्ञ step.
whatIfs.answer: Yes, profoundly. यज्ञ in this verse means selfless, well-directed action. Removing it would make the chain mechanical — any action produces rain. The verse's claim is that only SELFLESS action (yajña) keeps the cycle whole. Greed-action breaks it. The middle link is the moral heart.

realWorldExamples.title: Breakfast
realWorldExamples.body: Aria looks at her plate: rice, dal, vegetable, chapati. She traces the chain backward. The rice came from a paddy field. The paddy was fed by rain. The rain came in monsoon. The monsoon depends on forests, oceans, climate. कर्म → यज्ञ → पर्जन्य → अन्न → भूत. The Gītā's verse was at her breakfast table.

realWorldExamples.title: The drought news
realWorldExamples.body: A news story: parts of India facing drought, crop yields down, food prices up. Aria thinks of the Gītā chain. When rain (पर्जन्य) fails, food (अन्न) fails, beings (भूत) suffer. The verse is not abstract; it is a description of reality with consequences.

realWorldExamples.title: Composting at home
realWorldExamples.body: Aria's mother starts a kitchen compost. Vegetable peels go in; in a few months they come out as soil. The cycle from भूत back to soil to अन्न back to भूत is visible in a small bucket on the balcony. The Gītā wrote it down 2,500 years ago.

mnemonics.unpacking: Gītā 3.14: action → sacrifice → rain → food → beings. The cycle of creation in five words.
Here ब्रह्म = neuter, the Absolute (not the creator-god Brahmā). Same as in the Īśopaniṣad chapter.
जानीयात् ("should know"), कुर्यात् ("should do"), पठेत् ("should read"). The -ईयात्/-एत् ending = "ought to".
mnemonics.context: When you see a soft moral "should" form

deepDive.title: अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि — a verse straight from the Bhagavad Gītā
deepDive.body: The chapter's title is verse 3.14 of the भगवद्गीता, and the Gītā states it as one link in a great cycle: अन्नाद्भवन्ति भूतानि (from food, beings arise), पर्जन्यादन्नसम्भवः (food from rain), यज्ञाद्भवति पर्जन्यः (rain from sacrifice), यज्ञः कर्मसमुद्भवः (sacrifice from action). Beings → food → rain → यज्ञ → action → beings: a wheel (चक्र) that keeps the world turning, where each part owes its existence to the next. The Gītā's point is ethical as much as ecological — one who takes from this cycle without giving back, the next verse says, 'lives in vain'. The Gītā itself is 700 verses set within the Mahābhārata, Krishna's counsel to Arjuna on duty, action and devotion, and among the most translated books on Earth. Meeting one of its verses in Class 7 means the simple words 'from food, beings come to be' carry, in their home text, a whole philosophy of interdependence and selfless action (कर्मयोग).
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you understand the food-rain-sacrifice cycle the verse describes.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In senior classes you study the भगवद्गीता's teaching of कर्मयोग and the यज्ञ-cycle of which this verse is a part.

deepDive.title: जानीयात् — the optative (विधिलिङ्) for 'one should'
deepDive.body: जानीयात् means '(one) SHOULD know', and that flavour of advice, duty or possibility lives in a special mood called the विधिलिङ् (optative or potential). Where the present tense जानाति simply reports 'he knows', the optative जानीयात् prescribes 'he ought to know / let him know'. Sanskrit uses this mood constantly for rules and good counsel: सत्यं वदेत् ('one should speak the truth'), धर्मं चरेत् ('one should practise dharma'), न हिंस्यात् सर्वभूतानि ('one should not harm any creature'). The tell-tale marker is the -ई-/-या- that slips in before the ending (भवति → भवेत्, पठति → पठेत्). Because so much Sanskrit literature — dharmaśāstra, subhāṣitas, instructions of every kind — is phrased as 'one should', the optative is one of the most useful moods to recognise. Once you spot the विधिलिङ्, you can tell a command or recommendation apart from a plain statement of fact at a glance.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can read जानीयात् as 'one should know'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 8 you learn the विधिलिङ् (optative) of common roots and use it to express 'should / ought'.

deepDive.title: रसायनशास्त्रम् — how Sanskrit coins words for modern science
deepDive.body: The chapter's 'modern touch' word रसायनशास्त्रम् (chemistry) shows a living power of Sanskrit: building precise new technical terms from old roots, the way English reaches for Greek and Latin. रसायन (rasa, 'fluid/essence' + ayana, 'course') was the alchemy-and-elixir branch of आयुर्वेद, and शास्त्रम् means 'science/discipline', so the compound neatly names the science of substances. The same method generates a whole modern vocabulary: दूरभाषः (telephone, 'far-speech'), संगणकः (computer, 'the calculator'), विद्युत् (electricity), आकाशवाणी (radio, 'voice from the sky'), and दूरदर्शनम् (television, 'far-seeing'). Because Sanskrit words are transparent — each part means something — a coined term often explains itself. This is why Sanskrit has been proposed as a clear, unambiguous language for terminology, and why scientific Hindi borrows its vocabulary wholesale from Sanskrit roots. Seeing रसायनशास्त्रम् taken apart teaches you that you can often GUESS a Sanskrit technical word's meaning from its pieces.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you know रसायनशास्त्रम् means 'chemistry'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In later study you see how Sanskrit roots and compounds supply the technical vocabulary of modern Indian science.

bossQuestions.prompt: अन्नाद् भवन्ति भूतानि is the opening line of verse 3.14 of which text?
solutionSteps: The chapter states this is the opening line of Gītā 3.14.
It describes the cosmic food-cycle of creation.
So the source is the Bhagavad-gītā.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse it with the Īśopaniṣad line (ईशावास्यम्) of sch07 — this verse is from the Bhagavad-gītā.

variations.answer: from food, (living) beings come into being
solutionSteps: अन्नात् = 'from food'; भूतानि = 'beings'; भवन्ति = 'come to be'.
So: from food, beings arise.

bossQuestions.prompt: In अन्नाद् भवन्ति, the form अन्नाद् (from अन्नात्) is in which case, meaning 'from'?
solutionSteps: The sense 'from food / out of food' marks origin or source.
'From / origin' is the ablative case (पञ्चमी विभक्ति).
The अकारान्त ablative ending is -आत् (अन्न → अन्नात्, here sandhi'd to अन्नाद्).
commonMistakes: 'By/with' would be तृतीया and 'to/for' चतुर्थी — but 'FROM' (origin) is specifically the ablative पञ्चमी.

solutionSteps: 'From / out of' is origin.
That is the ablative, पञ्चमी विभक्ति.

bossQuestions.prompt: जानीयात् ('one should know') is in which mood, used for advice or duty?
solutionSteps: The sense 'one SHOULD know' expresses advice or obligation.
Sanskrit marks 'should' with the optative mood, विधिलिङ् (लिङ् लकार).
So जानीयात् is optative.
commonMistakes: 'One should know' is not a plain present ('knows') — the 'should' sense requires the optative mood.

variations.prompt: The Sanskrit mood used for 'should / ought to' is called…
solutionSteps: Advice/duty ('should') uses the optative.
It is the विधिलिङ् लकार.

bossQuestions.prompt: In this lesson ब्रह्म refers to…
options: the all-pervading cosmic source of all
bossQuestions.answer: the all-pervading cosmic source of all
solutionSteps: ब्रह्म (neuter) names the ultimate, all-pervading Cosmic Power.
The verse traces the food-cycle back to ब्रह्म as the source of all.
So ब्रह्म = the all-pervading source of everything.
commonMistakes: ब्रह्म (neuter, the Absolute) is not the same as ब्राह्मणः (a priest) — the words look alike but differ.

solutionSteps: भूतानि = 'beings, creatures'.
From food, the भूतानि arise.

bossQuestions.prompt: The chapter links the food-cycle to modern रसायनशास्त्रम्, which means…
solutionSteps: रसायन = 'chemistry'; शास्त्रम् = 'science/discipline'.
So रसायनशास्त्रम् = the science of chemistry.
The chapter connects the ancient food-cycle to modern chemistry.
commonMistakes: रसायनशास्त्रम् is specifically CHEMISTRY — the study of matter and reactions — not biology or astronomy.

solutionSteps: उत्पत्ति = origin, क्रमम् = order/sequence.
So: the order in which things come to be.

bossQuestions.prompt: उत्पत्तिक्रमम् describes…
options: the order in which beings come into existence
bossQuestions.answer: the order in which beings come into existence
solutionSteps: उत्पत्ति = 'coming into being / origin'; क्रमम् = 'order, sequence'.
So उत्पत्तिक्रमम् = the sequence of creation.
The verse lays out this chain: food → beings, rain → food, and so on.
commonMistakes: क्रमम् means 'order/sequence' — उत्पत्तिक्रमम् is about the ORDER of creation, not a herb or prayer.

solutionSteps: ओषधि = a herb; -ीनाम् = genitive plural ('of').
So ओषधीनाम् = 'of the herbs'.

chapters.title: दशमः कः? — Daśamaḥ Kaḥ? (Who Is the Tenth?)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 10. The classic Vedantic parable of the ten boys who cross a river: each one counts the others, forgets to count himself, and concludes the tenth has drowned — until a passing traveler tells the leader 'दशमः त्वम् असि' ('you are the tenth'). The chapter pairs this beautiful teaching story with an explicit grammar lesson on ordinal numbers (प्रथमः through दशमः), the gerund (तीर्त्वा), the imperfect past (अगणयत्), and the precise interrogative कतमः ('which of many?').

topics.title: दशमः कः? — The Tenth-Man Parable
topics.summary: The story and its Vedantic point: the seeker is the sought.

concepts.title: दशमः कः? — Who Is the Tenth?

explanations.oneLine: दशमः कः? — 'Who is the tenth?' — the famous Vedantic parable of ten travelers searching for the missing tenth.
explanations.kidFriendly: Ten boys swim across a river. After crossing, one boy counts to make sure all are safe — but counts only nine, forgetting to count himself. Every boy in turn does the same. Convinced the tenth drowned, they grow sad. A passing पथिकः (traveler) sees them, counts properly, and tells the leader 'दशमः त्वम् असि' — 'YOU are the tenth!' Joyful, they cry 'दशमः प्राप्तः' — the tenth is found!
explanations.textbook: The chapter's story: ten boys cross a नदी (river), each one of them counts only नव (nine), each विस्मरण (forgets) to count himself, all conclude दशमः नद्यां मग्नः ('the tenth drowned in the river'). A पथिकः (traveler) shows the leader 'दशमः त्वम् असि' — 'you are the tenth'.
explanations.expert: The story is a textbook Vedantic parable. The seeker IS the sought. The Self one searches for is the very Self that is searching. The famous Upaniṣadic 'तत् त्वम् असि' ('thou art that') shares the structure of 'दशमः त्वम् असि' ('thou art the tenth') — and the parable is its concrete picture.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses this beloved Indian parable to teach Sanskrit AND a deep philosophical idea — what we keep missing in our search is ourselves.

useCases.title: The point
useCases.description: The Self/seeker is what they were searching for the whole time.

useCases.title: Spot the line
useCases.description: दशमः त्वम् असि = 'YOU are the tenth' — the traveler's revelation.

useCases.title: Compare with Upaniṣad
useCases.description: Structurally parallel to 'तत् त्वम् असि' ('thou art That') of Chāndogya Upaniṣad.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The 'tenth man parable' (दशमस्त्वमसि) is one of Vedānta's classic teaching stories — used by Śaṅkara and many later commentators to illustrate the doctrine that the Self is never lost, only forgotten.

concepts.title: पथिकः — The Traveler / Teacher

explanations.oneLine: पथिकः (pathikaḥ) — 'a traveler, wayfarer'; in the parable, he plays the teacher's role.
explanations.kidFriendly: पथिकः means a traveler — someone walking the road. In the parable he plays the GURU's role: he sees the boys' confusion and reveals the truth they couldn't see for themselves. Glossary: मार्गगन्ता ('one who goes on the road').
explanations.textbook: पथिकः — 'traveler', glossed मार्गगन्ता. The chapter's pivotal figure: he counts properly and reveals दशमः त्वम् असि.
explanations.expert: पथिकः is from पथिन् ('path') + -इकः (agent suffix) — 'one of the path', a wayfarer. In Vedantic literature the शिक्षक / आचार्य often appears as a wandering पथिक — a chance teacher who reveals what was always there.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter makes पथिकः not just a passer-by but the catalyst — the outside voice that breaks the inner blindness.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet पथिकः in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 10; the glossary gives 'Traveler'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see पथिकः, recall it means 'Traveler'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using पथिकः ('Traveler').

concepts.beyondTheBook: In Indian story-tradition the chance पथिक (wayfarer) is a recurring figure of grace — wandering monks, wise strangers, the unexpected outside view that reveals what one couldn't see oneself.

concepts.title: मग्नः — Submerged / Drowned

explanations.kidFriendly: मग्नः means 'sunk' or 'drowned'. In the story the boys mistakenly conclude दशमः नद्यां मग्नः — 'the tenth has drowned in the river'. Glossary: विलीनः ('dissolved/submerged').
explanations.textbook: मग्नः — 'submerged/drowned', glossed विलीनः. Past-participle of मज्ज् ('to sink/dive'); used by the boys in their (false) conclusion about the missing tenth.
explanations.expert: मग्नः is the past-participle of मज्ज् ('to sink, dive'). The same root behind मज्जन ('plunging, bathing'). Used metaphorically for being 'immersed' in something — like being 'मग्न' in studies or grief.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses मग्नः to give the false conclusion its drama: the boys' wrong answer is vivid and final-sounding — yet completely mistaken.

useCases.title: Read it in the chapter
useCases.description: You meet मग्नः in NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 10; the glossary gives 'Drowned / submerged'.

useCases.title: Recognise the meaning
useCases.description: When you see मग्नः, recall it means 'Drowned / submerged'.

useCases.title: Use it in a sentence
useCases.description: Try a simple Sanskrit sentence using मग्नः ('Drowned / submerged').

concepts.beyondTheBook: मग्न is also used positively in Sanskrit — विद्यामग्न ('absorbed in learning'), ध्यानमग्न ('absorbed in meditation'). The same word names a dangerous submersion or a desirable absorption.

concepts.title: विषण्णाः → प्रहृष्टाः — From Sad to Delighted

explanations.oneLine: विषण्णाः (saddened) → प्रहृष्टाः (delighted) — the parable's emotional arc.
explanations.kidFriendly: The story's emotional arc: when they think the tenth drowned, the boys become विषण्णाः (saddened, dejected). When they realise the tenth is themselves — प्रहृष्टाः (delighted, overjoyed). The same group of people, no factual change in the river, just clear seeing turns sadness into joy. Glossaries: विषण्णाः = खिन्नाः ('sad'); प्रहृष्टाः = आनन्दिताः ('delighted').
explanations.textbook: विषण्णाः (saddened, glossed खिन्नाः) → प्रहृष्टाः (delighted, glossed आनन्दिताः). The chapter contrasts the two: same situation, different understanding, opposite emotion.
explanations.expert: Both are past-participles used as adjectives. विषण्णाः from वि+षद् ('to sink down, despair'); प्रहृष्टाः from प्र+हृष् ('to thrill with joy'). The same Bhagavad-Gītā arc: अर्जुन-विषाद (despair) → understanding → आनन्द.

concepts.reasoning: The parable's punch comes from this swing: they were never actually in trouble, just in misunderstanding. Right seeing instantly turns sadness into joy.

useCases.title: Same place, two emotions
useCases.description: Nothing in the river changed — only their seeing. That is the parable's whole point.

useCases.title: Spot the past-participles
useCases.description: विषण्ण (sad) and प्रहृष्ट (delighted) are both -त past-participles used as adjectives.

useCases.title: Gītā parallel
useCases.description: Arjuna's विषाद-योग (depression) opens the Gītā; clear seeing is its medicine.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The pair विषाद → आनन्द (despair → bliss) is one of Indian philosophy's great arcs — recurring from the Gītā to modern teachings on misperception and self-recognition.

questions.prompt: How many boys went to bathe in the river?
solutionSteps: The exercise: कति बालकाः स्नातुं गताः? Answer: दश.
The whole parable depends on the number being TEN.
commonMistakes: The story is specifically about TEN boys (दश) — that is why one being 'missing' matters.

solutionSteps: The exercise: कः सम्यक्‌रूपेण बालकान्‌ गणितवान्‌? Answer: पथिकः.
Glossary: पथिकः = मार्गगन्ता ('traveler').
Each boy missed himself; only the OUTSIDE viewer (पथिकः) counted right.
commonMistakes: The boys themselves kept making the SAME mistake — only the passing पथिकः counted correctly.

questions.prompt: Who turned out to BE the tenth?
solutionSteps: The traveler revealed: दशमः त्वम् असि — 'you are the tenth'.
Each counter had forgotten to count HIMSELF.
Exercise: दशमः कः आसीत्‌? Answer: नायकः.
commonMistakes: The 'missing' tenth was right there — the SELF, the one who was searching.

questions.prompt: What body of water did the boys cross?
solutionSteps: The chapter says they तीर्त्वा (having swum) पारं गताः (crossed) the नदीम् (the river).
Exercise: बालकाः कां तीर्त्वा पारं गताः? Answer: नदीम्.
commonMistakes: The chapter is specific about a NADI (river), not a pond or sea.

topics.title: Ordinals, Gerunds & Past Tense
topics.summary: प्रथमः…दशमः, तीर्त्वा (gerund), अगणयत् (imperfect past), कतमः (which-of-many).

concepts.title: प्रथमः, द्वितीयः, तृतीयः … दशमः — Ordinal Numbers

explanations.oneLine: Ordinal numbers in Sanskrit: प्रथमः (1st), द्वितीयः (2nd), तृतीयः (3rd), … दशमः (10th).
explanations.kidFriendly: Sanskrit makes ordinal numbers (first, second, third…) from the cardinals. The chapter explicitly teaches: एकम् → प्रथमः (1st), द्वे → द्वितीयः (2nd), त्रीणि → तृतीयः (3rd), and so on through दशमः (10th). Each has masculine/feminine/neuter forms: प्रथमः/प्रथमा/प्रथमम्.
explanations.textbook: पूरणार्थे ('for ordinals'): प्रथमः (1st), द्वितीयः (2nd), तृतीयः (3rd), चतुर्थः (4th), … दशमः (10th). Each has three genders (e.g. प्रथमः/प्रथमा/प्रथमम्).
explanations.expert: Sanskrit ordinals are mostly built with -थ, -ष, or -म suffixes on the cardinal stem (with stem changes): एक → प्रथम (irregular), द्वि → द्वितीय (-तीय), त्रि → तृतीय (-तीय), चतुर् → चतुर्थ (-थ), पञ्चन् → पञ्चम (-म), and so on. दशन् → दशम (10th, -म) is exactly the title's word.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter packages the parable WITH a grammar lesson: while you read 'who is the tenth?' you also learn how to say first/second/third up to tenth.

useCases.title: Count properly
useCases.description: प्रथमः → द्वितीयः → तृतीयः → चतुर्थः → पञ्चमः → षष्ठः → सप्तमः → अष्टमः → नवमः → दशमः.

useCases.title: Three genders
useCases.description: प्रथमः (m.), प्रथमा (f.), प्रथमम् (n.) — same for every ordinal.

useCases.title: Story link
useCases.description: 'दशमः' = 'the tenth' is the title word — the parable's whole punchline rides on this ordinal.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Indian ordinals leave traces in everyday Hindi: प्रथम (first), द्वितीय (second), तृतीय (third) — and in compounds like प्रथम-पुरुष ('first person' in grammar).

concepts.title: तीर्त्वा — Having Swum (Across)

explanations.kidFriendly: तीर्त्वा means 'having crossed/swum'. The boys तीर्त्वा (having swum) the river पारं गताः (crossed to the other side). Glossary: सन्तरणं कृत्वा ('having performed swimming').
explanations.textbook: तीर्त्वा — gerund (क्त्वान्त) of तॄ ('to cross'), glossed सन्तरणं कृत्वा. The gerund-in-त्वा / -ya describes a completed prior action: 'having crossed, they reached'.
explanations.expert: Sanskrit gerunds (formed -त्वा for un-prefixed roots, -य for prefixed) are everywhere in narrative. तीर्त्वा (तॄ + त्वा) is one form; पाठयित्वा ('having read'), कृत्वा ('having done') are others. The gerund neatly links two actions in one sentence.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses तीर्त्वा to describe the river-crossing that sets the whole parable in motion.

useCases.title: Two actions, one sentence
useCases.description: तीर्त्वा पारं गताः = 'HAVING crossed, they reached the other side' — gerund links.

useCases.title: Same root
useCases.description: तॄ ('to cross') → तीर्त्वा (gerund), तीर्थम् ('crossing-place, sacred ford').

useCases.title: In context
useCases.description: The story begins: ten boys 'तीर्त्वा' crossed the river — and the trouble starts after.

concepts.beyondTheBook: तीर्थ (sacred place) comes from the same root तॄ ('to cross') — a तीर्थ was originally a literal river-crossing, later a place where one 'crosses over' from this world to the spiritual.

concepts.title: अगणयत् — He Counted (Imperfect Past)

explanations.kidFriendly: अगणयत् means 'he counted' — a past-tense verb. Each boy अगणयत् (counted) the others but forgot himself, so each got नव (nine) instead of दश (ten). Glossary: गणनां कृतवान् ('did the counting').
explanations.textbook: अगणयत् — imperfect (लङ्) of the causative of गण् ('to count'), 3rd-singular. Glossed गणनां कृतवान्. The augment अ- + reduplication-less imperfect of the causative stem गणय-.
explanations.expert: लङ् (imperfect) marks ordinary past action ('counted'). Its formula: augment अ- + stem + secondary endings. गण् ('count') → causative गणयति ('makes count' / 'counts up') → imperfect 3rd-sg अगणयत्. Compare अकुर्वन् ('they did'), अवदत् ('he spoke').

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses अगणयत् repeatedly to walk through each boy's wrong count — building tension before the traveler's correct count.

useCases.title: Past-tense marker
useCases.description: The leading अ- (augment) is the giveaway of imperfect past.

useCases.title: Same root
useCases.description: गण् → गणयति (counts), गणितम् (mathematics), गणित (counted).

useCases.title: In story
useCases.description: Each boy अगणयत् — counted only 9, missing himself.

concepts.beyondTheBook: गण् ('count') is the root behind गणित — 'mathematics' literally means 'what has been counted/reckoned'. Even modern Indian languages call mathematics gaṇit.

concepts.title: कतमः vs कतरः — 'Which?' (of many vs of two)

explanations.oneLine: कतमः (katamaḥ) — 'which one (of many)'; distinct from कतरः ('which of two').
explanations.kidFriendly: कतमः means 'which one' — but specifically 'which out of MANY'. The chapter's exercise asks कतमः बालकः नद्यां मग्नः? — 'which (out of the many boys) drowned?' Sanskrit distinguishes कतमः (of many) from कतरः (of two). Glossary: कियत्-संख्यात्मकः ('of what number').
explanations.textbook: कतमः — 'which (of many)?', glossed कियत्-संख्यात्मकः. Distinct from कतरः which means 'which of two'. A subtle but real distinction Sanskrit makes.
explanations.expert: Sanskrit's interrogatives are more precise than English's 'which': कः ('who'), कतरः ('which of two'), कतमः ('which of many'). The -म suffix on कतमः is the same superlative-style suffix used in ordinals like दशमः — picking ONE out of many.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter chooses कतमः carefully — asking 'which (of the ten) boys drowned?' — a question only कतमः properly puts.

useCases.title: Pick the right 'which'
useCases.description: कतरः for two, कतमः for many — Sanskrit refuses to be vague.

useCases.title: In exercise
useCases.description: कतमः बालकः = 'which boy (of the ten)' — कतमः not कतरः.

useCases.title: Compare endings
useCases.description: दशम (10th) and कतम (which-of-many) share the -म suffix.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Sanskrit's care about 'of how many' shows in its dual number (forms specifically for two), its कतर / कतम distinction, and many other pairs — it is a language allergic to ambiguity.

solutionSteps: दश (cardinal 'ten') → दशमः (ordinal 'tenth', with -म suffix).
Masculine; feminine दशमा, neuter दशमम्.
commonMistakes: दश is the cardinal 'ten'; दशमः is the ORDINAL 'tenth' (with -म).

questions.prompt: 'तीर्त्वा' is what kind of word, and what does it mean?
options: a verb in present tense — 'he crosses'
solutionSteps: Glossary: तीर्त्वा = सन्तरणं कृत्वा ('having performed swimming').
-त्वा suffix marks a Sanskrit gerund: 'having done X'.
commonMistakes: The -त्वा ending is the gerund — 'HAVING crossed' (a prior completed action).

solutionSteps: Glossary: अगणयत् = गणनां कृतवान् ('did the counting').
The leading अ- (augment) is the past-tense (imperfect) marker.
commonMistakes: The अ- augment marks PAST (imperfect) — 'he counted', not present or future.

solutionSteps: Glossary: कतमः = कियत्-संख्यात्मकः ('of what number') — i.e. 'which one'.
Sanskrit distinguishes कतमः (of many) from कतरः (of two).
commonMistakes: कतमः is specifically WHICH-of-many — a different word from कः ('who') or कुतः ('whence').

glossary.example: पथिकः (pathikaḥ) — 'a traveler, wayfarer'; in the parable, he plays the teacher's role.
मग्नः (magnaḥ) — 'submerged, drowned, immersed'.
विषण्णाः (saddened) → प्रहृष्टाः (delighted) — the parable's emotional arc.
तीर्त्वा (tīrtvā) — 'having swum/crossed' (a gerund).
अगणयत् (agaṇayat) — 'he counted'; the imperfect-past tense.
कतमः (katamaḥ) — 'which one (of many)'; distinct from कतरः ('which of two').

misconceptions.kidsThink: It can be read as a queue position.
misconceptions.actually: Vedāntic reading: 'YOU are the tenth (the missing one you've been looking for).' The traveler's revelation is metaphysical — the SELF is what was missing all along. The parable serves Vedānta's तत्त्वमसि tradition. Reading it as just queue-ordering misses the depth.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Same as above but at the literal level.
misconceptions.actually: Yes, ordinally 'tenth' — but each boy thought the tenth was MISSING. The point is that the missing tenth was the COUNTER. The parable depends on each boy forgetting to count himself. The label 'tenth' is positional; the WHO of the tenth is the discovery.
गण् (कलनम्) = to count, enumerate. Different root from गा (sing). Listen for the consonant: गण् vs गा. Different roots, totally different families. गणयति 'he counts'; गायति 'he sings'.

misconceptions.kidsThink: It could look like a proper noun.
misconceptions.actually: पथिकः = 'a wayfarer / traveler'. Common noun, not name. Sanskrit forms common nouns with -इकः suffix often: पथिकः (wayfarer), यायावरः (wanderer), अध्वगः (traveller). The chapter's पथिकः is anonymous — the unnamed wayfarer is the parable's teacher figure.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Surprise is one of the emotions in the scene.
misconceptions.actually: प्रहृष्टाः = delighted, overjoyed (from हृष् 'to thrill with joy'). Sanskrit distinguishes आश्चर्य (surprise), विस्मय (wonder), and हर्ष (joy). The boys' state on discovering the tenth is HARSHA — joy at recovering what was 'lost.'

ncertQA.question: कति बालकाः स्नातुं गताः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: दश। (ten) The chapter's opening line: 'दश बालकाः नदीं तीर्त्वा पारं गताः' — ten boys crossed the river to bathe. The whole parable depends on the number being TEN.

ncertQA.question: कतमः बालकः नद्यां मग्नः इति निश्चयम् अकुर्वन्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: दशमः। (the tenth) Each boy counted only नव ('nine') and concluded the dasama (tenth) had drowned. But each boy was forgetting to count HIMSELF — each had been the tenth.

ncertQA.question: दशमः कः आसीत्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: नायकः / स्वयं गणकः। (the leader himself — the counter who kept forgetting to count himself) The traveller's revelation 'दशमः त्वम् असि' ('you are the tenth') points at the counter himself. The Self that was being searched for was the Self that was searching.

ncertQA.question: कः सम्यक्‌रूपेण बालकान्‌ गणितवान्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: पथिकः। (the wayfarer / traveller) Only the OUTSIDE viewer — the पथिकः (मार्गगन्ता) — counted properly. Each boy was blinded by trusting his own count without checking it from outside.

ncertQA.question: बालकाः कां तीर्त्वा पारं गताः?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: नदीम्। (a river) The chapter specifies a नदी (river), crossed by तरण (swimming). The गерund तीर्त्वा ('having crossed') marks the action that sets the parable in motion.

scientists.name: Adi Śaṅkarācārya
scientists.oneLineLegacy: The same Vedāntic master who first used the Tenth-Man parable as a teaching tool for तत्त्वमसि.
scientists.narrative: Śaṅkara also appears in Chapter 7 (Īśopaniṣad). For this chapter — the Tenth-Man parable — his role is even more direct: Śaṅkara and the Advaita Vedānta tradition he systematised used this very parable to illustrate the great saying तत् त्वम् असि ('thou art That') from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. The boys searching for the missing tenth are the seekers searching for the Self; the traveller is the guru who points; the discovery that 'I am the tenth' is the recognition तत् त्वम् असि. The parable's compactness and force made it a favourite teaching device of Vedāntic monks. When you read the parable as Sanskrit class material, you are reading one of Śaṅkara's preferred metaphors.

miniProjects.title: Find Your Own 'Tenth' Moment This Month
steps: For one month, watch for moments where you were searching for something you already had — keys in your pocket, a skill you already used, a friend who was always there.
Each time you catch yourself, write a one-line note. Just the situation.
Optionally: tell a friend about one of these moments. Sometimes the 'traveller' role of the parable is just talking to someone.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: By month's end you will have 5–10 'tenth' moments documented. The parable becomes a lens; you start using it on yourself.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: Vedānta's claim was that the deepest 'lost' thing — the Self — is the one always at hand. This exercise practices that pattern at smaller scales until it becomes habitual.

whatIfs.question: An obvious counting method that would have caught the mistake.
whatIfs.answer: Because each one trusted his own count more than the obvious procedure. Pride in one's own seeing is the very thing the parable critiques. The story works because the boys' OWN method is what blinds them — not stupidity but self-trust without checking. The Vedāntic point: we trust our own perception of the world (which leaves us out) and miss the obvious.

whatIfs.question: Suppose nobody pointed it out. They go home, mourn the lost tenth.
whatIfs.answer: Eventually someone would notice — a parent counting heads at home, perhaps. The parable does not say truth is hidden forever; it says SEEING it requires either an outside perspective or careful self-questioning. The 'traveler' role can be played by a teacher, a book, a difficult moment, a friend. Without them, blindness is much stickier.

whatIfs.question: A different shape of the same confusion.
whatIfs.answer: Then there would be NO Vedāntic truth to discover — the boys were correct that there was no tenth. The parable's force depends on there being a tenth they keep missing. Vedānta is making a specific claim: there IS a self each of us is missing. Not an absence, but a presence we don't see.

realWorldExamples.title: Looking for the keys
realWorldExamples.body: Aria searches the kitchen, the bedroom, the bathroom. Her keys are missing. She calls her brother for help — he points: 'They're in your hand.' Aria laughs. The Tenth-Man parable just happened. She had the keys all along; she had counted everywhere except where they were.

realWorldExamples.title: In meditation
realWorldExamples.body: Aria tries a short meditation. Her mind wanders. She tries to find 'the meditator who is supposed to be calm' — and realises she IS the meditator. She doesn't have to find herself; she is already there. The chapter said this would happen.

realWorldExamples.title: Helping a friend
realWorldExamples.body: A friend says, 'I'll never be good at maths.' Aria says, 'You did better than half the class on the last test — look at the report.' The friend looks. The friend stops searching for an imagined missing self. Sometimes you ARE the tenth, and someone just has to point.

mnemonics.unpacking: The tenth-man parable is a teaching tool for "you are That" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad). Same shape: thou art the missing one.
दशम (10th), षोडशम (16th) — the -म ordinal suffix on cardinals. Compare अष्टम (8th), नवम (9th).
कतमः = "which of many"; कतरः = "which of two". Sanskrit refuses the ambiguity English's "which" carries.

deepDive.title: 'You are the tenth' — the parable as a Vedānta teaching
deepDive.body: Ten boys cross a river, each counts the others, finds only nine, and grieves for a lost companion — until a wise passer-by points and says दशमस्त्वमसि: 'YOU are the tenth.' Vedānta teachers have told this story for centuries because it is a perfect image of the central Upaniṣadic insight. The counter overlooks the very self that is doing the counting, exactly as a person searches everywhere for happiness and meaning while overlooking their own true Self (आत्मन्). The teacher's words echo the महावाक्य तत्त्वमसि ('That thou art') from the छान्दोग्योपनिषद् — the truth was never missing, only unrecognised. Vidyāraṇya's पञ्चदशी uses precisely this 'tenth man' (दशम) example to explain how self-knowledge is not the GAINING of something new but the removal of an error. So the charming children's puzzle in your textbook is also one of the most elegant teaching-stories in Indian philosophy: what you seek, you already are.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can retell the parable and its surprise — the counter forgot himself.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In senior study you meet तत्त्वमसि and the Vedāntic use of the 'tenth man' parable to teach self-knowledge.

deepDive.title: तीर्त्वा — the क्त्वा gerund for 'having done X'
deepDive.body: तीर्त्वा means 'having crossed/swum across', and that '-ing first, then…' sense comes from the क्त्वा (ktvā) suffix, the Sanskrit gerund or absolutive. It marks the EARLIER of two actions by the same doer: स्नात्वा भुङ्क्ते means 'having bathed, he eats' (i.e. he bathes, THEN eats); पठित्वा गच्छति, 'having studied, he goes'. The ending appears as -त्वा (गत्वा 'having gone', कृत्वा 'having done', दृष्ट्वा 'having seen'). There is one important twist: when the verb carries a prefix (उपसर्ग), the क्त्वा changes to -य, the ल्यप् form — so from आ + गम् you get आगत्य ('having come'), and from वि + हस् you get विहस्य ('having laughed'). The gerund lets Sanskrit chain a sequence of actions tidily without repeating 'and then'. Recognising तीर्त्वा as 'having crossed' is your key to reading narrative Sanskrit, where these -त्वा / -य forms string the events of a story together.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can read तीर्त्वा as 'having swum across'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 8 you study the क्त्वा (gerund) and its prefixed form ल्यप् (-य) to link successive actions.

deepDive.title: अगणयत् — the imperfect past (लङ्) and its tell-tale अ-
deepDive.body: अगणयत् means 'he counted', a past-tense form, and the clue to its pastness sits right at the front: the little अ- prefix called the अट् augment (आगम). Sanskrit's everyday past tense is the लङ् लकार (imperfect), and it is built by putting अ- before the stem and adding past endings — so the present गणयति ('he counts') becomes अगणयत् ('he counted'), पठति → अपठत्, भवति → अभवत्, गच्छति → अगच्छत्. That leading अ- is the single most reliable signpost of the imperfect: see a verb beginning with अ that is not part of the root, and you are almost certainly looking at a past action. (Sanskrit actually has three past tenses — लङ् imperfect, लिट् perfect, लुङ् aorist — but the अ-augmented लङ् is the one stories use most.) Once you can strip the अट् augment off अगणयत् to find the familiar present stem, reading past-tense narrative becomes far easier.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can read अगणयत् as the past 'he counted'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 9 you learn the लङ् (imperfect) with its अ-augment and contrast it with the present and future.

bossQuestions.prompt: In दशमः कः?, ten travelers each count only nine. Why does each miss one?
options: the teacher hid one of them
solutionSteps: After crossing the river, each man counts the others but leaves HIMSELF out.
So each counts only nine and fears the tenth has drowned.
The teacher shows each is himself the missing tenth.
commonMistakes: No one actually drowned — the 'missing tenth' is the counter himself, whom each forgot to include.

variations.prompt: The teacher's lesson 'दशमः त्वम् असि' ('you are the tenth') means…
variations.answer: the one you seek is yourself
solutionSteps: Each counter overlooked himself.
So 'you are the tenth' — the sought one was never lost.

bossQuestions.prompt: The parable 'Who is the tenth?' is a famous teaching from which tradition, showing that the Self one seeks is already present?
options: Vedānta (the Self is never truly lost)
bossQuestions.answer: Vedānta (the Self is never truly lost)
solutionSteps: The chapter presents this as a famous Vedāntic parable.
It teaches that what one frantically searches for — the Self — is already here.
So the tradition is Vedānta.
commonMistakes: Though it involves counting, the parable's POINT is Vedāntic (about the Self), not a maths puzzle.

variations.prompt: The 'tenth man' you search for, in the parable, stands for…
solutionSteps: Each man forgot himself.
The tenth is the Self, never actually missing.

bossQuestions.prompt: Which is the correct Sanskrit ordinal for 'tenth'?
solutionSteps: दश is the CARDINAL 'ten' (how many).
Adding the ordinal suffix gives दशमः = 'tenth' (which position), masculine.
So the ordinal 'tenth' is दशमः.
commonMistakes: दश means 'ten' (the count); दशमः means 'tenth' (the rank) — the title asks दशमः कः, 'who is the TENTH?'

solutionSteps: प्रथमः = 'first'.
Then द्वितीयः (2nd), तृतीयः (3rd), … दशमः (10th).

bossQuestions.prompt: तीर्त्वा ('having crossed / swum') is which kind of verb form?
solutionSteps: तीर्त्वा ends in -त्वा, the gerund (absolutive) suffix क्त्वा.
It means 'having crossed', an action done BEFORE the main verb.
So it is a gerund.
commonMistakes: The -त्वा ending marks a gerund ('having ___ed'), not a tense — the men, 'having crossed', then counted.

variations.prompt: The gerund suffix that means 'having ___ed' is…
solutionSteps: -त्वा forms the gerund/absolutive.
तीर्त्वा = 'having crossed'.

bossQuestions.prompt: अगणयत् ('he counted') is in which tense?
solutionSteps: अगणयत् begins with the augment अ-, the mark of past tense.
It is the imperfect (लङ् लकार), 3rd-person singular.
So it means 'he counted' in the past.
commonMistakes: The leading अ- augment signals PAST tense — the present 'he counts' would be गणयति, with no अ-.

variations.prompt: The leading अ- on अगणयत् signals which time?
solutionSteps: The अ- augment marks past tense.
So अगणयत् = 'he counted' (past).

bossQuestions.prompt: कतमः asks 'which one?' — out of how many?
solutionSteps: Sanskrit distinguishes 'which of two' from 'which of many'.
कतमः asks 'which one of MANY (three or more)?'.
कतरः, by contrast, asks 'which of the TWO?'.
commonMistakes: कतमः (of many) and कतरः (of two) are a precise pair — don't use कतमः when choosing between just two.

variations.prompt: कतरः asks 'which?' out of how many?
solutionSteps: कतरः = 'which of the two'.
कतमः = 'which of many'.

chapters.title: द्वीपेषु रम्यः द्वीपोऽण्डमानः — Dvīpeṣu Ramyaḥ Dvīpo'ṇḍamānaḥ (Among Islands, the Beautiful Andaman)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 11. A classroom dialogue tours the Andaman Islands — their beauty (white sand, coral reefs, coconut palms), and their solemn history: the Cellular Jail (कालापानी), the three-storied prison built by the British, where Veer Savarkar bore ten years of suffering for India's freedom. The chapter names the four indigenous tribes of the islands (Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa, Sentinelese) and weaves in vocabulary (द्वीपः, कारागारम्, सोढवान्, जनजातिः) alongside Indian history and geography.

topics.title: The Andamans — Beauty & Freedom-Struggle History
topics.summary: Islands, Cellular Jail / Kālāpāni, Veer Savarkar, the four indigenous tribes.

concepts.title: द्वीपोऽण्डमानः — The Andaman Islands

explanations.oneLine: द्वीपोऽण्डमानः — 'the Andaman island(s)' — the most beautiful of India's islands.
explanations.kidFriendly: The chapter celebrates the Andaman Islands (अण्डमानद्वीपः) — among India's most beautiful (आकर्षकम्) island groups, with white sand (श्वेतरेणुः), coral reefs (प्रवालप्रस्तरैः), coconut palms (नारिकेलाः) and rich biodiversity. The title literally means 'among islands (द्वीपेषु), the beautiful island is Andaman'.
explanations.textbook: अण्डमानद्वीपः — the Andaman Island. The chapter introduces it as रम्यः (delightful), with white sand, transparent waters and coral reefs. The Andaman & Nicobar group is India's eastern island territory in the Bay of Bengal.
explanations.expert: द्वीपोऽण्डमानः shows visarga sandhi: द्वीपः + अण्डमानः → द्वीपोऽण्डमानः (the avagraha ऽ marks elided अ). द्वीपः literally means 'two-watered' (द्वि + अप्) — an island, surrounded by water on both/all sides.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches the student about a real, beautiful part of India — its eastern island territory — through Sanskrit.

useCases.title: Locate it
useCases.description: The Andaman & Nicobar Islands are India's territory in the Bay of Bengal, east of the mainland.

useCases.title: Break the word
useCases.description: द्वि ('two') + अप् ('water') = द्वीप ('island' — water on both sides).

useCases.title: Spot the sandhi
useCases.description: द्वीपः + अण्डमानः → द्वीपोऽण्डमानः (visarga + अ → ओ ऽ).

concepts.beyondTheBook: The Andaman Islands today are part of India's Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar; the chapter takes students on a Sanskrit tour of this real place.

concepts.title: सेल्युलर कारागारम् — The Cellular Jail (Kālāpāni)

explanations.oneLine: सेल्युलर कारागारम् / कालापानी — the colonial-era prison on Port Blair where India's freedom-fighters were jailed.
explanations.kidFriendly: On the Andamans is the famous सेल्युलर कारागारम् (Cellular Jail), also called कालापानी ('Black Waters'). Built by the British as a त्रितलात्मकम् कारागारम् (three-storied prison) to imprison Indian freedom-fighters (क्रान्तिकारिणः). Just hearing 'Kālāpāni' (कालापानी इति शब्दं श्रुत्वा) struck भीतिः (fear) — exile to this prison was the harshest punishment.
explanations.textbook: सेल्युलर कारागारम् ('Cellular Jail') = कालापानी, a त्रितलात्मकम् कारागारम् (three-storied prison) built by the British to imprison क्रान्तिकारिणः (revolutionaries) fighting for India's स्वातन्त्र्यम्.
explanations.expert: कारागारम् (prison) is कारा ('cell') + गारम् ('house'); सेल्युलर refers to the design — each prisoner in a separate cell to prevent communication. The 'Kālāpāni' name (literally 'black waters') reflected the dread of being shipped over the seas to permanent exile.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches not just Sanskrit but a vital piece of Indian history — what India's freedom cost, and where some of it was paid.

useCases.title: Know the name
useCases.description: Cellular Jail = कालापानी = colonial prison in Port Blair, Andamans.

useCases.title: Why feared
useCases.description: कालापानी ('black waters') meant being shipped beyond the seas to permanent exile.

useCases.title: Three storeys
useCases.description: त्रितलात्मकम् = त्रि + तल + आत्मकम् ('three-storied').

concepts.beyondTheBook: The Cellular Jail today is a national memorial; visitors light a सायं-ज्योतिः (evening light-and-sound show) to honour the freedom fighters who suffered there.

concepts.title: वीर सावरकर — A Hero of Freedom

explanations.oneLine: स्वातन्त्र्यवीरः सावरकरः — Veer Savarkar, who bore ten years' घोरम् कष्टम् (terrible suffering) in the Cellular Jail.
explanations.kidFriendly: The chapter names the महान् देशभक्तः, स्वातन्त्र्यवीरः सावरकरः (great patriot, freedom-hero Savarkar). For मातृभूमेः रक्षणाय (to protect the Motherland), he sोढवान् (bore) dश वर्षाणि (ten years) of कल्पनातीतं घोरं कष्टम् (suffering beyond imagination) in the Cellular Jail.
explanations.textbook: स्वातन्त्र्यवीरः सावरकरः — 'Freedom-hero Savarkar'. The chapter records that he सोढवान् (bore) ten years of imprisonment in the Cellular Jail for India's independence. (मुकुन्दः, a student-character in the dialogue, says: 'Blessed are those freedom-heroes; we live in peace because of their बलिदान — sacrifice.')
explanations.expert: सोढवान् is the past-active-participle (-तवत्) of सह् ('to bear/endure'). दश वर्षाणि = 'ten years' (वर्षम् in neuter plural). The chapter's framing is historical: it does not embellish, just records the fact of his decade in Cellular Jail.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter places Veer Savarkar's name and his sacrifice into the student's Sanskrit reading — turning a language lesson into a memorial.

useCases.title: Know the fact
useCases.description: Veer Savarkar bore ten years in the Cellular Jail for India's freedom.

useCases.title: Spot the verb
useCases.description: सोढवान् = '(he) bore/endured' — past participle of सह्.

useCases.title: Pay respect
useCases.description: The chapter's student line: 'we live in peace because of their बलिदान (sacrifice)'.

concepts.title: जनजातयः — The Indigenous Tribes

explanations.oneLine: अण्डमानी, ओङ्गी, जारवा, सेण्टिनली — the four indigenous जनजातयः (tribes) named in the chapter.
explanations.kidFriendly: The chapter names four विशिष्टाः जनजातयः (special tribal communities) of the Andamans: अण्डमानी (Andamanese), ओङ्गी (Onge), जारवा (Jarawa), सेण्टिनली (Sentinelese). These are some of the oldest continuous communities in the world — and India safeguards their आजीविका (livelihood). Glossary: जनजातिः = गणजातिः ('tribal community').
explanations.textbook: Andaman जनजातयः: अण्डमानी, ओङ्गी, जारवा, सेण्टिनली. The chapter notes that the government (सर्वकारः) takes care of their आजीविका (livelihood) — a real Indian policy concern reflected in the lesson.
explanations.expert: जनजातिः = जन ('people') + जाति ('class/community') — a 'people-community', i.e. a tribe. The Sentinelese in particular are studied as one of the world's most isolated populations, untouched by mainstream civilisation; India's protection law makes their island legally inaccessible.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches respect for India's indigenous diversity — naming these tribes inside a Sanskrit class is an act of recognition.

concepts.title: द्वीपः + प्रवालप्रस्तरैः — Island & Coral Reefs

explanations.oneLine: द्वीपः (island) + प्रवालप्रस्तरैः (by coral reefs) — the chapter's geographical vocabulary.
explanations.kidFriendly: द्वीपः means an island; प्रवालप्रस्तरैः ('by coral reefs') describes one of the Andamans' natural treasures. The chapter paints the islands with detail: श्वेतरेणुः (white sand), पारदर्शी (transparent waters), प्रवालप्रस्तरैः (coral reefs), नारिकेलाः (coconut palms).
explanations.textbook: द्वीपः (island, glossed अन्तरीपः), प्रवालप्रस्तरैः (by coral reefs, glossed विद्रुम-शिलाभिः). Other islands-vocabulary: श्वेतरेणुः (white sand), पारदर्शी (transparent), नारिकेलम् (coconut).
explanations.expert: प्रवालप्रस्तरैः is instrumental plural of प्रवाल-प्रस्तर ('coral-rock'). प्रवाल = 'coral'; प्रस्तर = 'rock/reef'. The Andaman corals are among the richest in the world — a real biological treasure the chapter names.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter packs the islands' geography into Sanskrit words — turning vocabulary practice into a virtual field trip.

concepts.title: कारागारम् + त्रितलात्मकम् — Prison & Three-Storied

explanations.oneLine: कारागारम् (prison) + त्रितलात्मकम् (three-storied) — naming the Cellular Jail's structure.
explanations.kidFriendly: कारागारम् means prison; त्रितलात्मकम् means 'three-storied' (तल = floor). The chapter uses these to describe the Cellular Jail's three-level structure. Glossary: कारागारम् = बन्धनगृहम् ('binding-house'); त्रितलात्मकम् = त्रिस्तरीयम्.
explanations.textbook: कारागारम् — 'prison', glossed बन्धनगृहम्. त्रितलात्मकम् — 'three-storied', glossed त्रिस्तरीयम्. Used together to describe the Cellular Jail's distinctive structure.
explanations.expert: कारागारम् = कारा ('cell/imprisonment') + गारम् ('house'). त्रितलात्मकम् = त्रि ('three') + तल ('floor/storey') + आत्मकम् ('having-as-nature') — 'three-floor-natured'. The Cellular Jail actually had radial wings of seven storeys originally; the chapter's three may refer to the central tower or watch-storey.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses these words to fix the physical reality of the Cellular Jail — not just a name, but a real building with cells and storeys.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The -आत्मकम् suffix ('having as nature/structure') is productive: द्व्यात्मकम् (two-natured), त्र्यात्मकम् (three-natured), and so on — vital for Sanskrit technical writing.

concepts.title: सोढवान् — He Bore (Past Active Participle)

explanations.kidFriendly: सोढवान् means 'he endured/bore' — a Sanskrit way of saying 'has borne'. The chapter uses it for Savarkar: कष्टं सोढवान् — 'he bore the suffering'. Glossary: सहनं कृतवान् ('did the bearing').
explanations.textbook: सोढवान् — masculine -तवत् past-active-participle of सह् ('to bear/endure'), glossed सहनं कृतवान्. Used as a finite verb meaning 'he has borne / he bore'.
explanations.expert: The -तवत् suffix (-तवान् m, -तवती f) makes 'one who has done X' from any verb root. सह् → सोढवान् ('one who has borne'). It carries an active sense, unlike the passive -त past participle. Compare कृतवान् ('having done'), उक्तवान् ('having said').

concepts.reasoning: The chapter uses सोढवान् to dignify Savarkar's suffering: not 'suffered' (passive) but 'bore it' (active, courageous).

concepts.title: जनजातिः — A Tribal Community

explanations.kidFriendly: जनजातिः means a tribal community — an indigenous people. The chapter names four such जनजातयः on the Andamans. Glossary: गणजातिः ('group-class').
explanations.textbook: जनजातिः — 'tribal community', glossed गणजातिः. A feminine i-stem noun; plural जनजातयः. The Indian government's term for officially-recognised indigenous communities is जनजाति (in Hindi/Sanskrit) or 'Scheduled Tribe'.
explanations.expert: जन ('people') + जाति ('birth-class, community') = 'a people-community'. The Constitution of India uses 'Scheduled Tribes' as the legal category; जनजाति is the everyday Hindi/Sanskrit word.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter introduces जनजातयः with respect — they are not curiosities but विशिष्टाः (special), and the सर्वकारः (government) looks after their आजीविका (livelihood).

सेल्युलर कारागारम् / कालापानी — the colonial-era prison on Port Blair where India's freedom-fighters were jailed.

misconceptions.actually: द्वीप = द्वि (two) + अप् (water) = land surrounded by water on BOTH sides → island. Sanskrit द्वीप literally means 'two-watered', but it names an ISLAND (one piece of land, water around). Same logic as Hindi द्वीप and English peninsula (almost-island).

जनजाति = tribal community (an officially recognised indigenous group). जनजाति has a precise legal meaning in modern India (Scheduled Tribe). It is NOT the same as 'common people' (आम जन / सामान्यजन). The chapter respects the legal/cultural specificity.

कारागार = PRISON (कारा = cell + गार = house). Don't confuse कारागार (prison) with कारखाना (factory, in Hindi) or विद्यागार (rare for library). The chapter's context — Veer Savarkar's ten years — makes clear it is a prison.

misconceptions.kidsThink: The English loanword may get Sanskritised oddly.
misconceptions.actually: 'Cellular' here is a direct English adoption for the prison's design (each prisoner in a separate cell to prevent communication). Sanskrit treats it as a foreign word. The Sanskrit version retains the English name 'Cellular' for the British architectural design — it has no Sanskrit-native synonym for that specific concept (the panopticon-like cell-by-cell layout).

कालापानी is a NAME for the Cellular Jail / the Andamans, NOT a sea or river. The metaphor: being shipped 'over the black waters' meant permanent exile from one's homeland. The name became the name of the prison itself. Translating it literally misses the cultural meaning.

scientists.name: Vīr Sāvarkar
scientists.oneLineLegacy: The freedom-fighter whose ten years in the Cellular Jail anchored the chapter's history.
scientists.narrative: Vinayak Damodar Savarkar, popularly known as Vīr Savarkar ('Hero Savarkar'), was sentenced to two life terms — fifty years total — in the Cellular Jail at Port Blair for his role in India's freedom movement. He served from 1911 to 1924, the brutal middle portion of which the chapter recalls. Inside the prison, with paper often forbidden, he composed thousands of lines of poetry — scratching verses on the walls with thorns or nails when no other means existed. After his release he became a controversial political figure (his Hindutva ideology remains debated to this day), but the chapter's reference is specifically to his prison-suffering for the Motherland's freedom — a fact about which there is no dispute.

whatIfs.question: Imagine the British had instead exiled freedom-fighters within the mainland.
whatIfs.answer: The Cellular Jail's brutality became powerful propaganda for the freedom movement — its existence galvanised opposition. A less spectacular exile might have created less moral pressure on British rule but also broken fewer revolutionary leaders. History rarely answers such counterfactuals cleanly; both directions are plausible.

whatIfs.question: Imagine the law protecting the Sentinelese were lifted and visitors allowed.
whatIfs.answer: Almost certainly catastrophe. The Sentinelese have no immunity to common diseases — even a single visitor's flu virus could be lethal to the tribe. India's protection law exists for this exact reason. The few attempts at contact (a documented 2018 case) ended badly. Sometimes the most respectful policy is distance.

whatIfs.question: Imagine he had died in confinement.
whatIfs.answer: His writing alone — poetry composed on prison walls, later political works — was substantial. He became a controversial figure post-independence, but the Cellular Jail's role as a National Memorial owes much to his eventual fame as a survivor. The chapter respects him for his ten years; history beyond the chapter is more complicated.

deepDive.title: कालापानी — the Cellular Jail and the freedom struggle
deepDive.body: The सेल्युलर कारागारम् (Cellular Jail) at Port Blair, dreaded as कालापानी ('the black water'), is one of the most sombre sites in India's freedom story. Built by the British and completed in 1906, its name comes from its design: seven wings of tiny solitary CELLS radiating from a central tower, so prisoners could neither see nor speak to one another. To this remote island the colonial government 'transported' revolutionaries — sentence to कालापानी meant exile across the sea, cut off from family and homeland, doing brutal labour like pressing oil at the kolhu. Among those imprisoned here was वीर सावरकर, who served years in its cells. After independence the jail became a national memorial; its walls carry the names of freedom fighters who endured it. So when your chapter tours the beautiful Andamans, it also asks you to remember their darker history — and the word त्रितलात्मकम् ('three-storied') in the lesson literally describes the jail's grim architecture.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you know सेल्युलर कारागारम् / कालापानी refers to the Andaman prison.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In later classes you study the history of the freedom struggle and the role of revolutionaries transported to the Andamans.

deepDive.title: सोढवान् — the past active participle (क्तवतु)
deepDive.body: सोढवान् means 'he (has) borne / endured', and it is not a finite verb but a past active participle, formed with the क्तवतु (-तवत्) suffix. This participle turns a verb into an adjective meaning 'one who has done X', agreeing in gender and number with its subject: from कृ ('do') comes कृतवान् ('he who has done'), कृतवती ('she who has done'); from गम् comes गतवान् ('he who has gone'). It pairs with its passive twin, the क्त (-त) past PASSIVE participle — कृतम् ('done'), गतः ('gone') — so Sanskrit can say either 'the boy who has eaten' (बालकः खादितवान्) or 'the food that was eaten' (अन्नं खादितम्). These participles let you express past actions compactly, often standing in for a full past-tense verb. Spotting the -तवत् ending in सोढवान् tells you instantly that someone HAS COMPLETED an action — here, the heroic endurance the chapter celebrates in those who suffered at the Cellular Jail.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can read सोढवान् as 'he bore / endured'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 8 you study the क्त and क्तवतु past participles (passive and active) and use them for past actions.

deepDive.title: प्रवालप्रस्तरैः — the instrumental plural and a descriptive compound
deepDive.body: प्रवालप्रस्तरैः ('with coral reefs') does two grammatical jobs at once. First, the -ऐः ending is the तृतीया (instrumental) PLURAL — the case that means 'by / with / by means of', here describing what the islands are adorned WITH. The instrumental is the workhorse for instruments and accompaniment (लेखन्या लिखति, 'he writes with a pen') and is governed by words like सह ('along with'). Second, प्रवालप्रस्तर is itself a compound: प्रवाल (coral) + प्रस्तर (rock/slab) = 'coral-rock', a कर्मधारय/तत्पुरुष joining the two nouns into one. So a single inflected word, प्रवालप्रस्तरैः, carries 'with [the] coral-rocks' — noun, adjective and preposition all folded together. Sanskrit's case endings make this possible: because -ऐः already says 'with, plural', no separate word for 'with' is needed. Unpacking प्रवालप्रस्तरैः into its compound and its case is exactly the two-step reading that long Sanskrit words always reward.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can read प्रवालप्रस्तरैः as 'with coral reefs'.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 9 and 10 you study the seven cases in full, including the तृतीया (instrumental) and its uses.

bossQuestions.prompt: सेल्युलर कारागारम्, also called कालापानी, was…
options: the colonial prison at Port Blair where freedom-fighters were jailed
bossQuestions.answer: the colonial prison at Port Blair where freedom-fighters were jailed
solutionSteps: सेल्युलर कारागारम् = the Cellular Jail, nicknamed कालापानी ('black water').
It stood on Port Blair in the Andamans.
India's freedom-fighters were imprisoned there in the colonial era.
commonMistakes: कालापानी / the Cellular Jail was a PRISON for freedom-fighters — not a temple or a park.

solutionSteps: कारागारम् = prison.
The Cellular Jail was such a कारागार.

bossQuestions.prompt: स्वातन्त्र्यवीरः सावरकरः is remembered in this chapter for…
options: enduring years of terrible suffering in the Cellular Jail
bossQuestions.answer: enduring years of terrible suffering in the Cellular Jail
solutionSteps: The chapter calls Savarkar a स्वातन्त्र्यवीरः ('hero of freedom').
He बोरे (सोढवान्) घोरम् कष्टम् — terrible suffering — during years in the Cellular Jail.
So he is remembered for that endurance.
commonMistakes: Savarkar is honoured for ENDURING imprisonment there, not for discovering or ruling the islands.

solutionSteps: सोढवान् is a past active participle of सह् ('to endure').
It means 'he bore / endured'.

bossQuestions.prompt: कारागारम् means…
solutionSteps: कारागारम् denotes a prison / jail.
The Cellular Jail is described as a कारागार.
So कारागारम् = prison.
commonMistakes: कारागारम् is a PRISON — not a fort (दुर्गम्) or temple (मन्दिरम्).

solutionSteps: द्वीपः = island.
The Andamans are द्वीपाः (islands).

bossQuestions.prompt: The Cellular Jail is described as त्रितलात्मकम् — meaning it is…
solutionSteps: त्रि = 'three'; तल = 'storey/floor'; -आत्मकम् = 'consisting of'.
So त्रितलात्मकम् = 'consisting of three storeys', three-storied.
It describes the jail's structure.
commonMistakes: त्रि is 'three' and तल is 'floor' — the word means three-STORIED, not three-cornered (triangular).

solutionSteps: त्रि is the prefix for 'three'.
त्रितल = three floors.

bossQuestions.prompt: सोढवान् ('he bore / endured') is which kind of form?
options: a past active participle ('one who has endured')
bossQuestions.answer: a past active participle ('one who has endured')
solutionSteps: सोढवान् ends in -वान् (the -तवत् past active participle).
It means 'he has borne / one who endured' — a completed past action by the doer.
So it is a past active participle.
commonMistakes: The -वान् / -तवत् ending marks a PAST ACTIVE participle, describing what the doer has already done.

variations.prompt: A participle ending in -वान् describes an action that is…
variations.answer: completed in the past (by the doer)
solutionSteps: -वान् (-तवत्) is the past active participle.
It marks a completed past action.

bossQuestions.prompt: The chapter names जनजातयः such as जारवा and सेण्टिनली. जनजातिः means…
solutionSteps: जन = 'people'; जाति = 'class/community'.
So जनजातिः = 'a people-community', i.e. a tribe.
जारवा and सेण्टिनली are indigenous जनजातयः of the Andamans.
commonMistakes: जनजातिः literally is 'people-class' = a TRIBE — not a reef or a bird.

variations.prompt: प्रवालप्रस्तरैः refers to the Andamans' famous…
solutionSteps: प्रवाल = coral, प्रस्तर = rock/reef.
So प्रवालप्रस्तरैः = 'by/with coral reefs'.

chapters.title: वीराङ्गना पन्नाधाया — Vīrāṅganā Pannādhāyā (Panna Dhai, the Brave)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 12. The historical story of Panna Dhai — the loyal wet-nurse (धाया) of Mewar's young prince Udai Singh II in the 16th century. When an evil-minded rival plotted to kill the prince in his sleep, Panna placed her OWN son in the prince's bed in his place, knowing her son would die — sacrificing her everything (सर्वस्वम्) to save the future king. The chapter honours her name 'in golden letters' (स्वर्णिमाक्षरैः) among India's brave women, while teaching vocabulary (धाया, छलेन, कुतन्त्रम्, शयनागारम्) and grammar (-तुम् infinitive of purpose, ordinal षोडशम्).

topics.title: पन्नाधाया — The Brave Wet-Nurse
topics.summary: Panna's identity, her supreme sacrifice, the 16th-century Mewar setting, and her place in golden letters.

concepts.title: पन्नाधाया — Panna Dhai, the Brave Wet-Nurse

explanations.oneLine: पन्नाधाया — Panna Dhai, the loyal Rajput धाया (wet-nurse) honoured as a वीराङ्गना (brave woman).
explanations.kidFriendly: Panna Dhai (पन्नाधाया) was the धाया — wet-nurse — of the young prince Udai Singh II of Mewar in the 16th century. The chapter honours her as a वीराङ्गना (brave woman) whose त्याग (sacrifice) saved the prince. धाया means 'wet-nurse' (Hindi धाय/दाई). Glossary: धाया = धात्री ('foster-mother').
explanations.textbook: पन्नाधाया — Panna Dhai, the धाया (wet-nurse) of Mewar's prince Udai Singh II in षोडशे शतके (the 16th century). The chapter honours her sacrifice as अद्वितीयम् (matchless) — written in स्वर्णिमाक्षरैः (golden letters) of history.
explanations.expert: पन्नाधाया is a name + role compound: पन्ना (her name) + धाया (wet-nurse, from धा 'to nourish'). The chapter places her among the वीराङ्गनासु — 'brave women' — at the top of the list, alongside other heroines of Indian history.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches an authentic piece of Indian history — Panna Dhai of Mewar — through Sanskrit, alongside the lesson of supreme त्याग (sacrifice).

useCases.title: Know the heroine
useCases.description: Panna Dhai of Mewar, 16th century, saved the prince's life by her sacrifice.

useCases.title: Break the word
useCases.description: पन्ना (her name) + धाया (wet-nurse, from धा 'to nourish').

useCases.title: In the list
useCases.description: The chapter lists her among वीराङ्गनासु — brave women whose names are written in golden letters.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Panna Dhai (पन्ना धाय) is remembered today in Rajasthan with statues, schools and a women's welfare scheme bearing her name — a continuing recognition of her sacrifice.

concepts.title: सर्वस्वत्यागः — Sacrificing One's Everything

explanations.oneLine: सर्वस्वम् (one's all) + त्यागः (sacrifice) — Panna Dhai gave her own son to save the prince.
explanations.kidFriendly: Panna Dhai's सर्वस्वत्यागः — sacrifice of everything — is the story's heart. When a दुष्टबुद्धिः (evil-minded) rival plotted to kill the young prince in his bedroom, Panna Dhai shायितवती (put to sleep) her OWN son in the prince's bed in his place — knowing her son would be killed. She gave सर्वस्वम् (her everything) for the king's son. Glossary: सर्वस्वम् = स्वीयं सम्पूर्णम् ('one's complete own').
explanations.textbook: सर्वस्वम् — 'one's all' (स्व + सम्पूर्णम्). The chapter narrates how Panna shायितवती ('put to sleep') her own son in the prince's शयनागारम् (bedroom) so the प्रतिस्पर्धी (rival) would kill her son instead of the prince — सर्वस्वत्यागः, sacrifice of everything.
explanations.expert: सर्वस्व is one's entire wealth/all; the chapter uses it absolutely — she didn't give wealth or even her own life, but the life of her own child, which is the deepest possible sacrifice. Compare दानम् (giving), त्यागः (renunciation), बलिदानम् (sacrifice — including life). सर्वस्वत्यागः is the most extreme.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches that the depth of a sacrifice is measured by what is given up — and Panna Dhai gave सर्वस्वम्.

useCases.title: Feel the weight
useCases.description: Panna gave her OWN son's life — that is what सर्वस्वम् means here.

useCases.title: Spot the verb
useCases.description: शायितवती = '(she) caused to sleep / put to sleep' — past active participle, causative of शी.

useCases.title: Compare
useCases.description: दानम् (gift) < त्यागः (renunciation) < बलिदानम् (life-sacrifice) < सर्वस्वत्यागः.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The motif of swapping a child in danger appears in many world stories (the Krishna-narrative's Nanda-Yashoda exchange, biblical Moses-in-the-bulrushes, etc.). What makes Panna's story specific is the certainty: she KNEW her child would die.

concepts.title: षोडशे शतके — In the Sixteenth Century

explanations.oneLine: षोडशे शतके — 'in the sixteenth century' (locative); placing Panna Dhai's story in real history.
explanations.kidFriendly: षोडशे शतके means 'in the 16th century'. The chapter dates Panna Dhai's story to the 1500s, the period of Mewar's Maharana lineage. Sixteen = षोडश; the locative form षोडशे शतके = 'in the 16th century'.
explanations.textbook: षोडशे शतके — locative of षोडशम् शतकम् ('the sixteenth century'). षोडश (16) is the cardinal; षोडशम् (with -म suffix) is the ordinal '16th', matching the ordinal pattern of Chapter 10 (दशमः etc.).
explanations.expert: षोडश = षष् ('six') + दश ('ten') = sixteen. The -म ordinal suffix gives षोडशम् ('sixteenth'). शतक = 'a group of hundred', so 'century'. The locative -ए (singular masculine/neuter) marks 'IN' the time period.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter places the story in real historical time — not myth — by dating it to the सोडशे शतके (16th century).

useCases.title: Date the story
useCases.description: 16th century — the time of Maharana Sanga's lineage in Mewar.
