By GENDER and ending: feminine nouns decline differently (आकारान्त रमा/लता, ईकारान्त नदी/मति), and so do neuters (फलम्, which has identical nominative and accusative — फलम् in both — a hallmark of neuter nouns). By the इ- and उ-ending masculines you already meet here (कवि, गुरु). The other great feature your three columns reveal is the द्विवचन — the DUAL number. Sanskrit counts in THREE numbers, not two: singular (एकवचन), dual (द्विवचन, for exactly two), and plural (बहुवचन, for three or more). So देवः / देवौ / देवाः means 'one god / two gods / many gods', each with its own endings throughout all seven cases. Mastering one paradigm gives you the template; the others are variations on the same seven-case, three-number grid.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can recite the देव (अकारान्त masculine) declension.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 8 and 9 you learn the feminine and neuter paradigms and use the dual (द्विवचन) confidently.

deepDive.title: सम्बोधनम् — calling someone, and the सुप् endings that attach
deepDive.body: The सम्बोधनम् (vocative) — हे देव! 'O god!' — is the form you use to ADDRESS or call someone, and Sanskrit grammar treats it as a special use of the प्रथमा (nominative): often it just shortens the nominative (देवः → हे देव), which is why declension tables list it beside the first case. All these case-endings — the marks that turn a bare stem like देव into देवः, देवम्, देवेन, देवाय … — are called the सुप् (sup) suffixes in Pāṇini's system: twenty-one endings (seven cases × three numbers) that the अष्टाध्यायी attaches by rule. A further wrinkle is that when words meet in a sentence, their final and initial sounds fuse by सन्धि (e.g. देवः + अत्र → देवोऽत्र), so reading real Sanskrit means UNDOING both the सन्धि and the सुप् ending to find the stem. Recognising the vocative and knowing that every ending is a सुप् suffix added to a stem is what lets you parse any inflected noun you meet.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can form the vocative (हे देव!) from the nominative.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In senior study you meet Pāṇini's सुप् (case-ending) system and how सन्धि fuses words at their boundaries.

bossQuestions.prompt: How many विभक्ति (cases) does Sanskrit have, besides the vocative?
solutionSteps: Sanskrit nouns decline through seven cases (विभक्ति): प्रथमा … सप्तमी.
The सम्बोधन (vocative, for calling) is counted separately.
So there are seven cases proper.
commonMistakes: The vocative is listed apart — the cases proper number SEVEN, not eight.

variations.prompt: The seven cases run from प्रथमा to…
solutionSteps: They are numbered प्रथमा (1st) … सप्तमी (7th).
So the last is सप्तमी.

bossQuestions.prompt: The nominative (प्रथमा) plural of देव is…
solutionSteps: देवः is the nominative SINGULAR; देवौ is the DUAL.
The nominative plural of an अकारान्त masculine adds -आः: देव → देवाः.
So 'the gods' (subject) = देवाः.
commonMistakes: देवान् is the ACCUSATIVE plural (object 'the gods'); the nominative (subject) plural is देवाः.

variations.prompt: The nominative singular of देव is…
solutionSteps: The nominative singular ending is -ः.
So देव → देवः.

bossQuestions.prompt: The प्रथमा (nominative) marks the subject; the द्वितीया (accusative) marks the…
solutionSteps: The nominative (प्रथमा) names the doer/subject.
The accusative (द्वितीया) names the object — what the action falls upon.
So द्वितीया marks the object.
commonMistakes: 'Means' is तृतीया, 'origin' पञ्चमी, 'location' सप्तमी — द्वितीया is specifically the OBJECT.

variations.prompt: In रामः ग्रामं गच्छति, which word is in the द्वितीया (object) case?
solutionSteps: रामः is the subject (nominative).
ग्रामम्, the goal/object, is accusative (द्वितीया).

bossQuestions.prompt: Which case means 'by / with' (the means or instrument of an action)?
solutionSteps: The 'by / with / by means of' relationship is the instrumental.
That is the तृतीया विभक्ति.
Example: हस्तेन ('with the hand').
commonMistakes: पञ्चमी (ablative) means 'FROM' (origin), not 'by/with' — the instrument is तृतीया.

solutionSteps: पञ्चमी marks origin or separation.
It means 'from'.

bossQuestions.prompt: The सप्तमी (locative) case answers which question?
solutionSteps: Each case answers a question.
The locative (सप्तमी) tells WHERE — in, on, or at a place.
Example: ग्रामे ('in the village').
commonMistakes: 'Of whom' (possession) is षष्ठी (genitive) — the locative (सप्तमी) is 'in/on/at', answering WHERE.

solutionSteps: षष्ठी marks possession, 'of'.
Example: रामस्य ('of Rama').

bossQuestions.prompt: हे देव! ('O God!') uses which form?
solutionSteps: Calling out to or addressing someone uses the सम्बोधन (vocative).
हे देव! ('O God!') is a direct address.
So it is the vocative form.
commonMistakes: The vocative (सम्बोधन, देव!) is for ADDRESSING — distinct from the nominative देवः, which names the subject.

variations.prompt: The case form used to call or address someone is the…
solutionSteps: Addressing someone uses the vocative.
हे देव! is in that form.

chapters.title: धातुरूपाणि — Dhāturūpāṇi (Verb Conjugation Tables)
chapters.summary: NCERT Class 7 Sanskrit (Deepakam) Chapter 15 — परिशिष्टम् २ (Appendix 2), the verb-conjugation reference. The appendix tables eight common Sanskrit roots (पठ्, अस्, कृ, श्रु, दा, ज्ञा, क्री, भाष्) across the लट् (present) tense in both parasmaipada and ātmanepada. This chapter introduces what a धातु (verb root) is, the लकार system of ten tense-moods, the two pada-classes (परस्मैपदम् vs आत्मनेपदम्), Sanskrit's three पुरुषs (note the reversed numbering — प्रथम = English 'third person'), and walks through paradigms of पठ् (read), अस् (be), कृ (do), and भाष् (speak).

topics.title: धातु, लकार, पद, पुरुष — The Verb System
topics.summary: Roots, the 10 लकाराs, parasmaipada vs ātmanepada, and Sanskrit's three persons.

concepts.title: धातुः — A Verb Root

explanations.oneLine: धातुः (dhātuḥ) — 'a verb root', the building-block of every Sanskrit verb form.
explanations.kidFriendly: धातु means a verb-root — the irreducible 'core' from which all the different forms of a verb are built. The appendix lists roots like पठ् (read), अस् (be), कृ (do), श्रु (hear), दा (give), ज्ञा (know), क्री (buy), भाष् (speak). Every Sanskrit verb you ever see traces back to one of these roots.
explanations.textbook: धातुः — 'verb root'. The classical Sanskrit grammar tradition (Pāṇini's धातुपाठ) enumerates around 2,000 roots organised into 10 गणाः (classes). The chapter samples eight common roots and shows their forms.
explanations.expert: Roots are usually monosyllabic (पठ्, गम्, कृ, दा) and end in a consonant or vowel. The grammarian's notation marks them with a virāma — पठ् (not पठ) — showing the bare root. From any धातु you derive: tenses (वर्तमान/भूत/भविष्यत्), moods (आज्ञा/विधि), participles (कृत), gerunds (कृत्वा), infinitives (-तुम्), agent nouns (-अक), etc. The root is the seed; the language is the tree.

concepts.reasoning: Knowing the धातु of a Sanskrit word is the master-key — once you know पठ् means 'read', forms like पठति (reads), पठितः (read, p.p.), पठितुम् (to read), पठनम् (reading) all open up.

useCases.title: Spot the root
useCases.description: Behind every Sanskrit verb form lurks a single short धातु.

useCases.title: Hundreds from one
useCases.description: From पठ् come पठति, पठतः, पठन्ति, अपठत्, पठेत्, पठितुम्, पठितः, पठित्वा, पठ्यते, पाठकः, …

useCases.title: Sample list
useCases.description: पठ्, अस्, कृ, श्रु, दा, ज्ञा, क्री, भाष् — the eight roots this appendix conjugates.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Pāṇini's धातुपाठ (the 'roots-recitation') lists about 2,000 Sanskrit verb roots — one of the world's first systematic linguistic catalogues, ~2,500 years old.

concepts.title: लकाराः — Sanskrit's Ten Tense-Moods

explanations.oneLine: लकाराः — the ten 'L-tenses' of Sanskrit (लट्, लङ्, लोट्, …), one per tense/mood.
explanations.kidFriendly: Sanskrit groups its tenses and moods into ten लकाराः — each named with a letter starting with ल-. The most-used: **लट्** (present, 'reads'), **लङ्** (imperfect past, 'read'), **लोट्** (imperative, 'read!'), **लृट्** (future, 'will read'), **विधिलिङ्** (optative, 'should read'). The appendix focuses on लट् (present).
explanations.textbook: लकाराः — tense-mood labels in Sanskrit grammar: लट् (present), लङ् (imperfect), लिट् (perfect), लुट् (periphrastic future), लृट् (simple future), लेट् (Vedic subjunctive), लोट् (imperative), विधिलिङ् (optative), आशीर्लिङ् (benedictive), लुङ् (aorist), लृङ् (conditional). Ten in all.
explanations.expert: Each लकार gets its own set of personal endings. The chapter focuses on लट् (वर्तमान — present): three persons × three numbers = 9 forms per root. The label 'ल' tags each tense-mood; the consonant after 'ल' (ट्/ङ्/ट्ओ/...) sets it apart.

concepts.reasoning: The लकार system gives Sanskrit one of the world's most regular tense-naming schemes: ten labels cover every standard tense/mood combination.

useCases.title: Five everyday ones
useCases.description: लट् (now), लङ् (then), लृट् (will), लोट् (do!), विधिलिङ् (should) — these cover most reading.

useCases.title: Name the slot
useCases.description: If you see लट्, the verb is PRESENT tense. The label IS the answer.

useCases.title: Pāṇinian system
useCases.description: Ten labels, each with a fixed meaning — Sanskrit grammar's tense-grid.

concepts.beyondTheBook: The 'ल-' naming convention is uniquely Sanskrit and reflects Pāṇini's love of compression: each tense is named by a single syllable. Modern grammarians elaborated, but the 'ल-' tags persist.

concepts.title: परस्मैपदम् vs आत्मनेपदम् — Two Voice Classes

explanations.oneLine: परस्मैपदम् ('for-another') and आत्मनेपदम् ('for-oneself') — Sanskrit's two padas.
explanations.kidFriendly: Sanskrit verb roots come in two families: **परस्मैपदम्** ('words for another') and **आत्मनेपदम्** ('words for oneself'). They use DIFFERENT endings. पठ् (read) is परस्मैपद; भाष् (speak) is आत्मनेपद. Some roots use both (उभयपद). The appendix shows both sets.
explanations.textbook: परस्मैपदम् — 'for-another' endings (active sense). Sample लट् (present) for पठ्: पठति/पठतः/पठन्ति (3rd), पठसि/पठथः/पठथ (2nd), पठामि/पठावः/पठामः (1st). आत्मनेपदम् — 'for-oneself' endings. Sample लट् for भाष्: भाषते/भाषेते/भाषन्ते etc.
explanations.expert: Originally परस्मैपद expressed 'action for another' (transitive sense) and आत्मनेपद 'action for oneself' (reflexive/middle). By Classical Sanskrit the distinction is largely lexical — each root just belongs to one or both classes, and you memorise which. Bhāṣ ('speak') is naturally a self-oriented action; पठ् (read) is naturally other-oriented — the pada-distinction sometimes still feels meaningful.

concepts.reasoning: The chapter teaches both pada-classes side by side so students recognise BOTH endings — पठति 'reads' AND भाषते 'speaks' — without being thrown by the second set.

useCases.title: Two-voice system
useCases.description: Sanskrit verbs come in TWO ending-families: parasmaipada and ātmanepada.

useCases.title: Memorise the pada
useCases.description: Each root belongs to one (or both); the lexicon tells you which.

useCases.title: Spot the ending
useCases.description: -ति → parasmaipada; -ते → ātmanepada. The third-singular present is the giveaway.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Greek had a similar 'middle voice'; English collapsed all its verbs into one paradigm. Sanskrit's two-pada system preserves a deep Indo-European feature: who benefits from the action — another, or yourself.

concepts.title: त्रयः पुरुषाः — Three 'Persons' in Sanskrit (and Beware — They Are Reversed)

explanations.oneLine: Sanskrit's three पुरुष: प्रथमपुरुष (he/she — 'third person'), मध्यमपुरुष (you — 'second'), उत्तमपुरुष (I — 'first').
explanations.kidFriendly: Sanskrit numbers its 'persons' the OPPOSITE WAY from English! What English calls 'first person' (I), Sanskrit calls उत्तमपुरुष ('best/last person'). What English calls 'third person' (he/she), Sanskrit calls प्रथमपुरुष ('first person'). And the 'second' (you) is मध्यमपुरुष ('middle person'). The order: he/she → you → I, not I → you → he/she.
explanations.textbook: प्रथमपुरुष = 'first person in the table' = he/she/it. मध्यमपुरुष = 'middle person' = you. उत्तमपुरुष = 'last person in the table' = I. Sanskrit verb tables are ordered प्रथम (he) at the top and उत्तम (I) at the bottom — the inverse of English grammar books.
explanations.expert: The Sanskrit ordering reflects how a sentence usually flows: someone speaks ABOUT a third party first, then addresses the listener, then themselves. The names refer to POSITION in the verb-table, not to importance. Pāṇini's ordering is consistent and used in every Sanskrit grammar; the 'first person = I' habit comes from Western grammar tradition.

concepts.reasoning: Knowing the Sanskrit ordering prevents a common confusion: when an Indian Sanskrit teacher says 'prathama-puruṣa', they mean HE/SHE (third person in English terms) — not I.

useCases.title: Don't get confused
useCases.description: Sanskrit's प्रथमपुरुष = English 'third person' (he/she).

useCases.title: Three forms each
useCases.description: Each पुरुष has three numbers: singular, dual, plural — 3×3 = 9 forms per tense.

useCases.title: Table-order
useCases.description: Sanskrit verb tables read top→bottom: he, you, I (the reverse of English textbooks).

concepts.beyondTheBook: The numbering reflects an old logical idea: in any conversation, the topic (someone/something) comes first, the addressee second, and the speaker last — Pāṇini just codified this in his table layout.

solutionSteps: धातु is the 'root' of a verb — its irreducible core.
Pāṇini lists about 2,000 roots in his धातुपाठ.
commonMistakes: Don't confuse with the chemistry usage; here धातु is a VERB ROOT.

questions.prompt: Which लकार stands for the PRESENT tense?
solutionSteps: लट्-लकार = वर्तमानकालः (present tense).
लङ् is past, लोट् is imperative, विधिलिङ् is optative.
commonMistakes: लट् is the PRESENT tense; the others are different tenses/moods.

questions.prompt: Which set of endings does the root 'पठ्' (read) take?
solutionSteps: पठ् → पठति (-ति ending) = परस्मैपद (active, 'for another').
भाष् → भाषते (-ते ending) would be आत्मनेपद.
commonMistakes: पठ् is parasmaipada (ending -ति in 3rd-sg present), not ātmanepada.

questions.prompt: In Sanskrit grammar, 'प्रथमपुरुष' (first person) refers to —
solutionSteps: Sanskrit orders persons OPPOSITELY from English: प्रथम = he/she.
'I' is उत्तमपुरुष (last in the Sanskrit table).
commonMistakes: Sanskrit's 'first person' (प्रथम) is the English THIRD person (he/she) — a famous reversal.

topics.title: Four Common Paradigms (पठ्, अस्, कृ, भाष्)
topics.summary: Present-tense conjugation of the four key roots students meet most often.

concepts.title: पठ् → पठति, पठतः, पठन्ति — Present of a Common Root

explanations.oneLine: पठ् in लट् (present), parasmaipada: पठति / पठतः / पठन्ति — 'he reads / they two read / they read'.
explanations.kidFriendly: The verb-root पठ् ('to read') in present tense: 3rd-person singular पठति ('he/she reads'), dual पठतः ('the two read'), plural पठन्ति ('they read'). 2nd-person: पठसि / पठथः / पठथ ('you / you two / you all read'). 1st-person: पठामि / पठावः / पठामः ('I / we two / we read').
explanations.textbook: पठ् धातुः, लट्-लकार (present), परस्मैपद. The endings, when added to the stem पठ्-: -ति/-तः/-न्ति, -सि/-थः/-थ, -मि/-वः/-मः. Apply these to almost any 1st-class (भ्वादि) parasmaipada root.
explanations.expert: These endings (-ति/-तः/-न्ति …) are some of the most common in classical Sanskrit. They mark not only tense but person + number in one suffix — a single ending tells you BOTH who and how many. Compare गच्छति ('he goes'), नयति ('he leads'), वदति ('he speaks') — all the same पठति pattern.

concepts.reasoning: Learn पठति's full nine forms and you can recognise the present tense of HUNDREDS of common Sanskrit verbs.

useCases.title: Nine forms, one tense
useCases.description: Three persons × three numbers = 9 forms per tense.

useCases.title: Sentence sample
useCases.description: छात्रः पुस्तकं पठति = 'the student reads a book'.

concepts.beyondTheBook: 1st-class (भ्वादिगण) roots — the largest class — all decline like पठ्. Memorising पठति-table is one of the highest-leverage things a Sanskrit student can do.

concepts.title: अस् → अस्ति, स्तः, सन्ति — The Verb 'To Be'

explanations.oneLine: अस् in present: अस्ति / स्तः / सन्ति — 'he is / they two are / they are'.
explanations.kidFriendly: अस् ('to be') is the most common verb in any language — and Sanskrit is no exception. Present-tense forms: 3rd-person अस्ति / स्तः / सन्ति; 2nd-person असि / स्थः / स्थ; 1st-person अस्मि / स्वः / स्मः. Note: this is an athematic (irregular) root, so the forms involve stem-changes (अस् → अस्ति but स्तः, सन्ति).
explanations.textbook: अस् is a 2nd-class (अदादि) root — athematic, meaning no thematic vowel between stem and ending. Present-tense full table includes irregular alternations (अस्ति vs स्तः). This is irregular enough that it must be memorised separately.
explanations.expert: अस् ('to be') is one of those critical irregular verbs every language seems to have — English 'is/am/are/be/was', French 'être/suis/est', Sanskrit अस्ति/अस्मि/सन्ति. Linguists trace all of these to the Proto-Indo-European root *h₁es- ('to be'). Same root, deep history.

concepts.reasoning: Of all Sanskrit verbs, अस्ति is the one to know FIRST — it appears in countless sentences and quotations.

useCases.title: Famous opening
useCases.description: 'अहम् अस्मि' = 'I am' — the simplest Sanskrit sentence.

useCases.title: All irregular
useCases.description: अस्ति (he is), अस्मि (I am), सन्ति (they are), स्थः (you two are) — memorise the whole set.

useCases.title: Universal root
useCases.description: Same root as English 'is', Latin 'est', French 'est' — all from PIE *h₁es-.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Every famous Sanskrit dictum uses अस्ति: सत्यम् अस्ति ('truth is'), विद्या एव सर्वस्वम् अस्ति ('knowledge alone is everything'). Recognising अस्ति/सन्ति is the threshold of reading.

concepts.title: कृ → करोति, कुरुतः, कुर्वन्ति — 'To Do'

explanations.oneLine: कृ in present: करोति / कुरुतः / कुर्वन्ति — 'he does / they two do / they do'.
explanations.kidFriendly: कृ ('to do/make') is another supremely common root. Present-tense (irregular!): 3rd-person करोति / कुरुतः / कुर्वन्ति; 1st-person करोमि / कुर्वः / कुर्मः. The stem-vowel shifts between करो-/कुर्व-/कुरु- in different forms — typical of 8th-class (तनादि) roots.
explanations.textbook: कृ धातुः, लट्-लकार, परस्मैपद. 8th-class (तनादि-gana). Present stem alternates: करो- (strong) before -ति/-मि, कुरु-/कुर्व- (weak) before consonant/plural endings.
explanations.expert: कृ's stem alternation looks complex but follows a regular pattern: 'strong' stem before singular endings, 'weak' before others. The same root gives countless derivatives: कार्यम् ('what is to be done'), कर्ता ('doer'), कर्म ('action'), कारणम् ('cause'), संस्कार ('refinement'), विकार ('change'), संस्कृति ('culture').

concepts.reasoning: Of all roots, कृ has perhaps the richest derivative-family in Sanskrit — knowing it is opening a major treasure-chest.

useCases.title: Stem alternation
useCases.description: Strong (करो-) before -ति/-मि; weak (कुरु-/कुर्व-) elsewhere.

useCases.title: Massive family
useCases.description: कर्म, कर्ता, कार्य, कारण, संस्कार — all from कृ.

useCases.title: Everyday sentence
useCases.description: 'अहं कार्यं करोमि' = 'I do the work'.

concepts.beyondTheBook: Sanskrit's word 'संस्कृत' itself comes from कृ — सम् ('together, well') + कृत ('done') = 'well-made/refined'. The language names itself with its most important verb.

concepts.title: भाष् → भाषते, भाषेते, भाषन्ते — An ātmanepada Sample

explanations.oneLine: भाष् in present (आत्मनेपद): भाषते / भाषेते / भाषन्ते — 'he speaks / the two speak / they speak'.
explanations.kidFriendly: भाष् ('to speak') is naturally an ātmanepada root. 3rd-person present: भाषते / भाषेते / भाषन्ते. Notice the endings: -ते / -एते / -अन्ते — quite different from parasmaipada's -ति / -तः / -न्ति. Other ātmanepada examples include सेव् (serve), लभ् (obtain), वन्द् (worship).
explanations.textbook: भाष् धातुः, लट्-लकार, आत्मनेपद. The ātmanepada present-tense endings: -ते/-एते/-अन्ते (3rd), -से/-एथे/-ध्वे (2nd), -ए/-वहे/-महे (1st). Distinct enough from parasmaipada to be unmistakable.
explanations.expert: The -ते (vs -ति) third-person-singular present is the easiest tell: see -ते and you've found an ātmanepada verb. Some roots actually use BOTH sets (उभयपद); the lexicon notes them as such.

concepts.reasoning: Recognising भाषते as 'he speaks' (and not getting confused that it doesn't end in -ति) is the chapter's practical pay-off — readers stop being thrown by the second voice.

useCases.title: Spot the -ते
useCases.description: -ते ending in 3rd-singular = ātmanepada. Don't confuse with parasmaipada's -ति.

useCases.title: Common ātmanepada
useCases.description: भाष् (speak), सेव् (serve), लभ् (obtain), वन्द् (worship) — all -ते.

useCases.title: Bhagavad-Gītā example
useCases.description: 'श्री-भगवान् उवाच' uses उच्/वच् with active sense; भाषते would be 'he speaks' in present.

concepts.beyondTheBook: When you encounter the famous Gītā verse 'श्री-भगवानुवाच' ('Lord Krishna SPOKE'), उवाच is a perfect tense of वच् — but the same idea in present would be भाषते or वदति, both 'speaks'.

questions.prompt: The 3rd-person singular present of the root 'पठ्' (to read) is —
solutionSteps: पठ् + ति (3rd-singular parasmaipada present) = पठति.
Means 'he/she reads'.
commonMistakes: पठति is SINGULAR; पठतः is dual, पठन्ति is plural, पठामि is 'I read'.

questions.prompt: The 1st-person singular present of the root 'अस्' (to be) is —
solutionSteps: अहम् अस्मि = 'I AM'.
अस्ति = he is; सन्ति = they are; आसीत् = he was (past).
commonMistakes: अस्मि is FIRST PERSON ('I am'); अस्ति is third person ('he is').

questions.prompt: The 3rd-person singular present of the root 'कृ' (to do) is —
solutionSteps: कृ + 3rd-singular present (parasmaipada) = करोति ('he does').
करोमि = 'I do'; कुर्वन्ति = 'they do'; कृतवान् = past p.p.
commonMistakes: करोति is the standard 3rd-singular form; the others are 1st-person, plural, or past.

questions.prompt: Which ending tells you a verb is ĀTMANEPADA in the 3rd-person singular present?
solutionSteps: 3rd-singular present: parasmaipada -ति, ātmanepada -ते.
Spotting -ते means 'middle voice' — a different family of endings.
commonMistakes: The DISTINGUISHING ending is -ते (vs parasmaipada -ति).

glossary.example: लकाराः — the ten 'L-tenses' of Sanskrit (लट्, लङ्, लोट्, …), one per tense/mood.
परस्मैपदम् ('for-another') and आत्मनेपदम् ('for-oneself') — Sanskrit's two padas.

glossary.definition: Three 'Persons' in Sanskrit (and Beware — They Are Reversed).
glossary.example: Sanskrit's three पुरुष: प्रथमपुरुष (he/she — 'third person'), मध्यमपुरुष (you — 'second'), उत्तमपुरुष (I — 'first').
पठ् in लट् (present), parasmaipada: पठति / पठतः / पठन्ति — 'he reads / they two read / they read'.
अस् in present: अस्ति / स्तः / सन्ति — 'he is / they two are / they are'.
कृ in present: करोति / कुरुतः / कुर्वन्ति — 'he does / they two do / they do'.
भाष् in present (आत्मनेपद): भाषते / भाषेते / भाषन्ते — 'he speaks / the two speak / they speak'.

misconceptions.actually: Sanskrit has 10 गण (verb classes) with different conjugation patterns. पठ् is class 1 (भ्वादि), the most common — but अस्, कृ, श्रु belong to other classes with different forms. Memorise पठ् as the standard, then learn the irregularities. The chapter's appendix shows pattern variations across classes — that's the point of multiple examples.

They use DIFFERENT endings. 3rd singular present: parasmaipada -ति (पठति) vs ātmanepada -ते (भाषते). Each verb root belongs to one (or both — उभयपद) pada-class. The lexicon tells you which. Mixing them gives wrong forms.

अहम् = 'I' → I-form needed: अहम् करोमि. करोति is 'HE does' (third person). Sanskrit verbs MUST agree with subject in person and number. अहम् (1st sing) → करोमि. तत्/सः (3rd sing) → करोति. आवाम् (1st dual) → कुर्वः. वयम् (1st pl) → कुर्मः.

misconceptions.kidsThink: अ- might look like the negative prefix.
misconceptions.actually: अ- here is the past-tense AUGMENT (लङ्-लकार). अकरोत् = 'he did' (past tense). Two different अ- in Sanskrit: (1) past-tense augment (अकरोत्), (2) negative prefix (अधर्मः = non-righteousness). Context tells you which. Past-tense verbs always have it.

misconceptions.kidsThink: Western grammar tradition orders 'I, you, he'.
misconceptions.actually: Sanskrit reverses it: प्रथमपुरुष = he/she (Western 3rd); मध्यमपुरुष = you (2nd); उत्तमपुरुष = I (1st). When an Indian grammarian says 'first person', they mean WHAT WESTERN BOOKS CALL THIRD PERSON. The reversal is consistent and historic — don't translate the term word-for-word.

ncertQA.question: लट्-लकारः कस्य कालस्य रूपाणि दर्शयति?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: वर्तमानकालस्य। (present tense) Among Sanskrit's ten लकाराः, लट् marks the present tense (वर्तमानकालः). Other key ones: लङ् (imperfect past), लोट् (imperative), लृट् (future), विधिलिङ् (optative).

ncertQA.question: 'पठ्' धातोः लट्-लकारस्य प्रथमपुरुष-एकवचनम् किम्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: पठति। पठ् (root, 'to read') + त्ति (3rd-singular present, parasmaipada) = पठति ('he/she reads'). Sanskrit's प्रथमपुरुष = English 'third person' (a famous reversal).

ncertQA.question: 'अस्' धातोः उत्तमपुरुष-एकवचनं लट्-लकारे किम्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: अस्मि। अहं अस्मि = 'I am'. The verb अस् ('to be') is athematic and irregular; अस्मि (1st sg), असि (2nd sg), अस्ति (3rd sg). Sanskrit's उत्तमपुरुष = English 'first person'.

ncertQA.question: 'भाष्' इति धातुः कस्मिन् पदे वर्तते?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: आत्मनेपदे। (in the ātmanepada class) भाष् ('to speak') is an ātmanepada root — its 3rd-singular present is भाषते (-ते ending), distinct from parasmaipada's -ति. The chapter's appendix shows both pada-classes side by side.

ncertQA.question: 'कृ' धातोः लट्-लकारस्य प्रथमपुरुष-बहुवचनम् किम्?
ncertQA.modelAnswer: कुर्वन्ति। कृ ('to do') — 8th class, stem alternates: करोति (3rd sg, strong stem करो-), कुरुतः (3rd dual, weak कुरु-), कुर्वन्ति (3rd pl, weak कुर्व-).

scientists.name: Patañjali
scientists.oneLineLegacy: Author of the Mahābhāṣya, the great commentary on Pāṇini's grammar.
scientists.narrative: Patañjali — distinct from the YOGA-sūtra Patañjali, though tradition often conflates them — wrote the Mahābhāṣya ('the great commentary') on Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī in around 2nd century BCE. The work is enormous: a sūtra-by-sūtra discussion of Pāṇini's rules, with examples, debates and refinements. The Mahābhāṣya is THE classical reference for understanding Sanskrit verb conjugation — the chapter's धातुरूपाणि. Patañjali clarifies tricky cases, defends Pāṇini against critics, and adds rules where Pāṇini was silent. The conjugations you learn from the chapter's tables ultimately trace back to Pāṇini's sūtras, with Patañjali's commentary as the bridge that makes them teachable.

miniProjects.title: Conjugate One New Verb You've Never Met
needs: The chapter's पठ् conjugation table for reference
steps: Pick any 1st-class (भ्वादिगण) parasmaipada root from any dictionary or hint: गम् (go), वद् (speak), जय् (conquer), नी (lead), क्षम् (forgive). All work.
Draw a 3x3 grid: rows = persons (3rd, 2nd, 1st); columns = numbers (sg, dual, pl).
Apply the पठ् endings to your root's stem: -ति/-तः/-न्ति, -सि/-थः/-थ, -मि/-वः/-मः.
Pronounce all 9 forms aloud.
Optionally: write 'I read', 'he reads', 'they read' in English next to the forms.
miniProjects.expectedObservation: Nine new Sanskrit verb-forms — generated by you from one rule.
miniProjects.whyItWorks: The chapter showed grammar IS a generator: learn one pattern, write hundreds of words. This exercise makes the generative power real.

whatIfs.question: Imagine a language with no past, no future — only present.
whatIfs.answer: Yes, but laboriously — via TIME PHRASES ('yesterday, he goes'). Mandarin Chinese does something close to this, marking time with words rather than verb endings. The strategy WORKS but offloads work from grammar onto vocabulary. Sanskrit's many tenses encode time precisely and quickly.

whatIfs.question: Sanskrit's अस् 'to be' is irregular. Imagine ALL ~2,000 roots were too.
whatIfs.answer: Barely. The whole point of regular conjugation patterns is that learning ONE verb in a class teaches you HUNDREDS. Irregularity is the price of frequency: the most-used verbs (be, do, go, eat) tend to be irregular in many languages because high-frequency use polishes them into unique shapes. Sanskrit's mostly-regular system is what makes 2,000 roots manageable.

whatIfs.question: Sanskrit was largely transmitted by memory long before being written down.
whatIfs.answer: Three things: (1) precise rules like Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, which is small enough to memorise; (2) intense oral training in gurukulas; (3) ritual contexts where mistakes were socially expensive. Without writing, those three substitutes had to do all the preservation. The fact that Sanskrit survived intact across millennia of oral-only transmission is one of human civilisation's quiet miracles.

realWorldExamples.title: Choosing the right verb-form
realWorldExamples.body: Aria wants to write 'I read' in Sanskrit. She knows पठ् is the root. Person: first (उत्तम). Number: singular (एकवचन). Tense: present (लट्). Answer: पठामि. She just used the chapter's grammar to construct a sentence she has never seen before. That's what grammar is for.

realWorldExamples.title: Recognising a Sanskrit news headline
realWorldExamples.body: A Sanskrit news headline reads भारतं सिद्धिं प्राप्तवान्. Aria sees the verb प्राप्तवान् — past active participle (-तवान् suffix, from प्राप् 'to obtain'). She decodes: 'India HAS OBTAINED success.' Grammar lets her read the news.

realWorldExamples.title: Pāṇini in modern code
realWorldExamples.body: Aria's older cousin shows her a paper comparing Pāṇini's grammar to formal grammars in computer science. Aria recognises Pāṇini's name from the chapter. A 2,400-year-old Indian grammarian helping define how computers parse code. The chapter prepared her for this surprise.

mnemonics.unpacking: पठति "he reads", करोति "he does", अस्ति "he is", भाषते "he speaks". -ति/-ते endings.
-ति = परस्मैपद (parasmaipada). -ते = आत्मनेपद (ātmanepada). The 3rd-singular ending tells you the voice.
प्रथमपुरुष = English "third person" (he/she). मध्यम = you. उत्तम = I. Sanskrit numbers from "topic" to "speaker".

deepDive.title: The ten गण — why not all verbs conjugate like पठ्
deepDive.body: पठति ('he reads') looks simple, but it hides a choice: every Sanskrit root belongs to one of TEN classes called गण (gaṇa), and the class decides how the present-tense stem is built. पठ् is a भ्वादि (first class) root, which inserts -अ- before the ending (पठ् + अ + ति = पठति) — the largest and most regular group, named after भू ('to be', भवति). Other classes behave differently: the अदादि (second class, like अस् 'to be' → अस्ति) add endings DIRECTLY to the root with no vowel; the चुरादि (tenth class, like चुर् → चोरयति) insert -अय-; the तुदादि, दिवादि, स्वादि and the rest each have their own stem-marker. This is why a conjugation table works for पठ्, नम्, गम् and वद् (all भ्वादि) but not blindly for अस् or कृ. Knowing a root's गण tells you in advance how to form its present, imperfect and imperative — turning what looks like memorising endless tables into applying ten predictable patterns.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you can conjugate पठ् → पठति, पठतः, पठन्ति in the present.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 9 you learn that roots fall into ten गण (classes), each forming its present stem differently.

deepDive.title: The लकार system — Sanskrit's ten tense-moods
deepDive.body: Sanskrit organises ALL of a verb's tenses and moods into ten sets of endings called the लकाराः, each named with a code-letter ल् plus a marker. The five you most need are लट् (present — पठति, 'reads'), लङ् (imperfect past — अपठत्, 'read', with its अ-augment), लृट् (future — पठिष्यति, 'will read'), लोट् (imperative/command — पठतु, 'let him read'), and विधिलिङ् (optative — पठेत्, 'should read'). Beyond these lie the more advanced लकाराः you meet later: लिट् (the perfect, for remote past — पपाठ), लुङ् (the aorist), लुट् (a periphrastic future), आशीर्लिङ् (the benedictive, for blessings), and लृङ् (the conditional, 'would have'). Each लकार is simply a complete kit of personal endings expressing one time-or-mood. Once you realise that learning a verb means learning which लकार you need — present to report, लोट् to command, विधिलिङ् to advise — the whole verb system becomes a tidy menu of ten choices rather than a fog of forms.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you know लट् (present) and have met a past and a future form.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 10 and beyond you study the full लकार system, adding the perfect, aorist, imperative and optative.

deepDive.title: परस्मैपद and आत्मनेपद — two families of verb endings
deepDive.body: Sanskrit verbs come in two voice-classes with DIFFERENT sets of personal endings: परस्मैपद (literally 'word for another') and आत्मनेपद ('word for oneself'). पठति, गच्छति, करोति take परस्मैपद endings (-ति, -तः, -न्ति), while भाषते ('speaks'), लभते ('obtains') and सेवते ('serves') take आत्मनेपद endings (-ते, -एते, -न्ते) — which is exactly why your paradigm भाष् → भाषते, भाषेते, भाषन्ते looks so different from पठ् → पठति, पठतः, पठन्ति. Historically आत्मनेपद hinted that the action's fruit returns to the doer (reflexive/middle voice), though in practice each root simply 'belongs' to one set, or to both (उभयपदी). All these endings are the तिङ् (tiṅ) suffixes in Pāṇini's grammar — eighteen forms (nine परस्मैपद + nine आत्मनेपद across three persons and three numbers). Knowing whether a root is परस्मैपदी or आत्मनेपदी tells you which ending-set to reach for, so you never confuse भाषते with a nonexistent *भाषति.
deepDive.prerequisite: Tackle this once you notice भाषते uses different endings from पठति.
deepDive.nextStepHint: In Class 8 and 9 you study परस्मैपद and आत्मनेपद endings (the तिङ् suffixes) and which roots take each.

bossQuestions.prompt: धातुः means…
solutionSteps: धातुः is the basic verb root from which all verb forms are built.
For example पठ् ('to read') is a धातु.
So धातुः = verb root.
commonMistakes: धातुः is a VERB root — nouns decline (शब्दरूप), but धातु is the building-block of verbs (धातुरूप).

variations.prompt: पठ्, the root behind पठति, is an example of a…
solutionSteps: पठ् is the verb root.
From it comes पठति ('he reads').

bossQuestions.prompt: Sanskrit's tenses and moods are organised into how many लकार ('L-tense/moods')?
solutionSteps: Each tense or mood has its own लकार (named लट्, लङ्, लोट्, लृट् …).
There are ten लकाराः in all.
So the answer is ten.
commonMistakes: There are TEN lakāras — not seven; लट् (present), लङ् (past), लृट् (future), लोट् (imperative) are just four of them.

solutionSteps: लट् लकार is the present tense.
पठति is in लट्.

bossQuestions.prompt: परस्मैपदम् means 'word for another'; आत्मनेपदम् means…
solutionSteps: पद here means a class of verb endings.
परस्मैपदम् = 'for another'; आत्मनेपदम् = आत्मने ('for oneself') + पद.
So आत्मनेपदम् = 'word for oneself'.
commonMistakes: आत्मने means 'for oneself' — the contrast is परस्मै ('for another') vs आत्मने ('for oneself'), not about tense.

variations.prompt: भाष् → भाषते is an example of which pada?
solutionSteps: भाषते uses आत्मनेपद endings (-ते).
So it is आत्मनेपद.

bossQuestions.prompt: पठति is 'he reads' (singular). How do you say 'they (many) read'?
solutionSteps: पठति is singular; पठतः is dual ('the two read').
The plural ('they all read') is पठन्ति.
So 'they read' = पठन्ति.
commonMistakes: पठतः is the DUAL ('they two read') — the plural ('they all read') is पठन्ति.

solutionSteps: पठतः is the dual form.
It means 'the two of them read'.

bossQuestions.prompt: The plural 'they are' from the root अस् ('to be') is…
solutionSteps: अस्ति = 'he/she/it is' (singular); स्तः = 'the two are' (dual).
The plural 'they are' is सन्ति.
So 'they are' = सन्ति.
commonMistakes: अस्ति is SINGULAR ('he is') and स्तः is dual — the plural 'they are' is सन्ति.

solutionSteps: अस्ति is the singular of अस्.
It means 'he/she/it is'.

bossQuestions.prompt: In Sanskrit's own naming, the प्रथमपुरुष ('first person') actually corresponds to which English person?
solutionSteps: Sanskrit numbers its 'persons' in the reverse of English.
प्रथमपुरुष (Sanskrit 'first') = English THIRD person (he/she/it).
उत्तमपुरुष (Sanskrit 'last/best') = English first person (I).
commonMistakes: The naming is reversed: Sanskrit's प्रथमपुरुष is English's THIRD person — a classic trap.

variations.prompt: The उत्तमपुरुष in Sanskrit corresponds to which English person?
solutionSteps: उत्तमपुरुष = English first person.
So it means 'I / we'.
